editorials.title: Deep rot: On the Election Commission of India’s functioning during its SIR
editorials.passage:
The investigation by The Indian Express into the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) functioning during its Special Intensive Revision (SIR) shows that the disquiet over what transpired under Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar ’s watch is not limited to civil society, the media and the Opposition . It ran through the ECI itself, as Election Commissioners (EC) Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi objected on record at least 14 times between October 2025 and August 2026 to decisions, many of which, they said, were taken without their knowledge. Their dissent mirrors what many have long said about the SIR. In May, Mr. Joshi had warned that Form 6, the application for new electors, could not be altered without the government amending the rules. Yet, in July, the form contained questions on whether the applicants or their parents or grandparents figured in the “electoral roll of the last SIR”, which Mr. Sandhu called “unauthorised and illegal”. The ECs also flagged the centralisation of the electoral roll database, sought an audit, and recorded that field officials lacked complete access to the ERONet portal. This mirrors what local election officials had complained of: that many of the changes in the rolls were done at the central database level overriding Electoral Registration Officers, the statutory authority on voters’ eligibility.

The consequences of the anomalies in the ECI’s decision-making and its functioning were the deepest in West Bengal. About 60 lakh electors were flagged for software-generated “logical discrepancies” — many were dubious — and 27 lakh names were deleted. Of the 38 lakh appeals pending before tribunals, 16.1 lakh were by those seeking to remove voters whom judicial officers had included; Mr. Sandhu’s question of who authorised filing them on the ECI’s behalf remains unanswered. Meanwhile, over nine in 10 appeals against deletion decided so far have restored the electors, which suggests that the exercise struck off lakhs of genuine voters before the West Bengal elections. The Hindu’s analysis also revealed that 24 of the 70 seats in Delhi now have fewer electors in draft rolls than those who actually voted just a year and a half ago. On Wednesday, Justice Dipankar Datta, as part of a two-judge Bench, held in his opinion that the 2023 Act’s replacement of the CJI, whom the Anoop Baranwal judgment had placed on the selection panel, with a Union Minister, fails the “perception test” . It was this panel that chose Mr. Kumar as CEC. Regrettably, the Supreme Court had earlier upheld the SIR without adequately confronting its design, which deletes electors before verification and places the burden of proving eligibility on the citizen rather than the state, thereby defeating the constitutional guarantee of universal adult franchise. Mr. Kumar must resign and the Court must halt further deletions until the roll database is audited. Anything less will be a defeat for India’s democracy.

editorials.title: Trading smart: On the India-New Zealand FTA
editorials.passage:
The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) , set to come into force on October 20 , is a good example of why India is right in simultaneously pushing for trade deals with smaller trade partners along with the major global economies. On the face of it, it would be easy to dismiss the $1.1 billion of bilateral goods trade between the two countries as being less than 1% of India’s total goods trade. A doubling by 2030, as envisaged under the deal, is still a minuscule amount. Yet, trade is not simply a macroeconomic indicator. It is also a source of livelihood for lakhs of businesses, nearly half of which are micro, small, and medium enterprises. These exporters need all the help that they can get in the current trade environment. Adverse developments related to tariffs or the closure of trade routes can be mitigated to an extent by a nimble rerouting of trade to other countries where Indian exporters receive an advantage. With 100% U.S. tariffs looming and a trade deal with Washington remaining elusive, India needs to open up as many alternative channels for its exporters as possible. The New Zealand FTA delivers — India has managed to receive duty-free access on 100% of its exports, a historic concession. India has a good mix of capital- and labour-intensive exports to New Zealand that stand to benefit. Textiles make up about 14% of India’s exports, while pearls and semi-precious stones constitute another 5% or so. On the capital-intensive side, one-third of India’s exports are pharmaceuticals, parts of nuclear reactors, vehicular parts, mineral fuels, electrical machinery, and iron and steel.

India has also done well in its handling of sensitive sectors. While the opening up of India’s dairy sector was a major demand by the New Zealand negotiators, India held firm and excluded it from the deal. In total, nearly 30% of India’s import lines have been kept outside the tariff concessions. On labour mobility, India has won some valuable concessions on visas for workers and students. At a time when several western countries are clamping down on foreign worker inflows, such alternative routes provide relief. India has also extracted a commitment from New Zealand to facilitate investments of $20 billion in India over 15 years, smaller but along the same lines as in the agreement with the EFTA bloc. India needs foreign investment not just for its economic growth but also to manage its balance of payments. This FTA is a good blueprint on how India can use its growing international heft to negotiate overwhelmingly in its favour.

editorials.title: The Election Commission of India needs to ensure unhurried SIR process in Delhi, speed in Bengal
editorials.passage: It’s deeply damaging for Indian democracy that the Election Commission of India regularly makes the headlines for unsavoury reasons. The charges range from inept revision of electoral rolls and disregard of complaints to selective application of the model code of conduct. The crescendo of complaints reached fever pitch this week as the Delhi SIR exercise revealed glaring lapses and the West Bengal SIR’s redress mechanism reported agonisingly slow progress.At the same time, pleas challenging the method of selecting election commissioners themselves came up in the Supreme Court. On Wednesday, Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma delivered a split verdict on referring the pleas to a Constitution Bench. The decision to constitute a larger bench now passes to the Chief Justice, whose replacement with a Union cabinet minister on the appointment panel is in question. Thus, the prospect of judicial delay clouds the horizon at a time crucial state elections loom large..The Delhi SIR stands out as much for how many were struck off the voters’ list as for who were among them. Of the 1.45 crore voters, about 47.6 lakh names were taken off and 31.6 lakh sent notices—together almost half the national capital’s electorate. Among the latter were a former Deputy PM, a former Vice President, current and previous Chief Ministers of the state, and current and former Union cabinet ministers. If senior officials are facing such glitches, it raises more worrying questions of common citizens’ status. Inconsistent methods of serving notices are a cause for concern, with a large section of voters reporting ignorance of being taken off the rolls. By Wednesday, less than 3 percent of them had applied for inclusion.In West Bengal, the latest numbers show it would take nearly 12 years for the ECI-appointed tribunals to address all disputed cases at the present rate of disposal. If an SC judge’s remark that some voters might have to skip one chance to vote seemed too casual for comfort, lakhs now face the prospect of missing two national elections.While the deadline for filing claims in Delhi needs to be extended beyond September 30, the opposite needs to happen in West Bengal. The ECI needs to ensure far greater efficiency in the tribunals’ work. editorials.title: Balance must in Western Ghats development plans
editorials.passage: A special session of the Karnataka legislature convened to discuss the Kasturirangan Committee report on the Western Ghats rejected its recommendations and sought modifications to the seventh draft notification issued by the Union Environment Ministry on July 27, 2026. The state has sought a year to conduct a fresh forest survey through a technical committee, along the lines of the Kerala model, and consult the Centre thereafter. All political parties in Karnataka oppose the notification, which proposes an Ecologically Sensitive Area (ESA) covering about 37 percent of the Western Ghats—59,940 sq km across six states. In Karnataka, this covers 20,668 sq km and 1,449 villages across 10 districts. Villagers fear displacement and loss of livelihood. The state is expected to formally respond by September 27, 2026.The report has been criticised for relying on remote sensing and satellite imagery from 2012 to demarcate ‘natural’ and ‘cultural’ landscapes. Given the changes since then, Karnataka’s proposal for a ground survey merits consideration. Kerala had adopted a similar approach through the Oommen V Oommen Committee, which conducted a survey and submitted its report in 2014, seeking changes to the proposed ESA. The National Green Tribunal subsequently granted relaxations and reduced its extent. Karnataka has maintained that people cannot be evicted, while making it clear that further encroachment and unregulated commercialisation cannot be allowed..The Kasturirangan panel submitted its report in 2013 after reviewing the 2011 Madhav Gadgil report, which had proposed declaring the entire 1,29,037-sq-km Western Ghats an ESA, with stringent restrictions on mining, farming, tourism, and thermal and hydel projects. Kasturirangan expanded the region under consideration to 1,64,280 sq km across six states, while excluding settlements, fields and plantations from the strictest restrictions. It recommended that mining and power projects be considered only after detailed ecological assessments.Karnataka will now have to strike a delicate balance between conservation and development. Recent floods and landslides underline the ecological risks. Mining, quarrying, road construction and tourism will have to remain within carefully managed limits. The Western Ghats, a Unesco biodiversity hotspot and home to 13 national parks and sanctuaries, must be protected without undermining the livelihoods of those who live there—and preserved for future generations..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | Wight through the looking-glass
editorials.passage: What does it say about a product’s safety concerns that its maker is considering launching a version without its most-used feature? Meta Platforms, which dominates the global market for smart glasses, is launching a pair without cameras. The company, which last year sold more than 70 lakh of these AI-assisted glasses co-developed with EssilorLuxottica, has been accused in the US and Europe of misleading consumers over a product that records video and audio of people and places without their consent. Such a backlash had forced pioneer Google to take its ‘Explorer’ glasses off the market about a decade ago. India today lacks a law regulating wearable devices such as these, relying instead on the ad hoc application of various statutes. editorials.title: Authority and respect
editorials.passage:
Two recent tragedies, though fundamentally different, force us to confront an uncomfortable question about the culture of our schools. In one incident, a very young child reportedly collapsed and died after allegedly being physically punished by a teacher over incomplete homework. The precise circumstances and medical cause require due investigation, but the allegation itself is deeply disturbing. 

In another incident, a school principal was reportedly killed in an alleged act of extreme violence involving students. The circumstances of that case too require careful investigation. These incidents should not be treated as mirror images. One concerns an alleged misuse of adult authority against a child; the other concerns alleged violence against an educator. Their legal and moral dimensions are different. Yet together they compel us to examine something larger: the culture of boundaries, responsibility, authority and human relationships within our educational institutions. 

A school is meant to be a place where children learn not only academic subjects, but also how human beings should treat one another. That places an enormous responsibility on every adult and every student within the school community. There was a time when physical punishment was casually accepted as part of schooling. Many adults grew up hearing that a teacher punished a child because the teacher cared. The flaw in that logic is exposed. A five- or six-year-old does not become a better learner because fear has entered the classroom. 

Fear may produce immediate compliance, but compliance is not learning, and obedience is not character. Teachers absolutely have a responsibility to correct children. Children need boundaries, routines and consequences. But correction must preserve dignity. There is a fundamental difference between telling a child, “This behaviour is unacceptable; let us work together to change it,” and making the child feel worthless or deserving of pain. 

Physical punishment, intimidation and public humiliation are not signs of strong pedagogy. They indicate that an adult has failed to find a more constructive way of exercising authority. This is particularly important in the early years. A child who enters school with curiosity should not gradually learn to associate the classroom with fear. The question every school leader should therefore ask is simple but difficult: have academic expectations ever been allowed to become more important than the emotional and physical safety of children? If the answer is yes, those practices and systems must change. 

Rejecting authoritarianism, however, does not mean rejecting authority. A teacher should never be permitted to hit or humiliate a child. Equally, a student cannot be permitted to threaten, intimidate or assault a teacher. A principal must be accountable for decisions, but accountability does not give students permission to retaliate violently when they disagree with an authority figure. Young people live in a world where disagreement is immediate, public and often amplified by social media. They see anger rewarded with attention and confrontation turned into entertainment. 

Schools cannot remain completely insulated from those influences. When disagreement becomes hostility, frustration becomes aggression and aggression becomes violence, the consequences can be devastating. Educators too are entitled to safety, dignity and protection. Respect for children cannot mean disrespect for adults. At the same time, respect for adults cannot mean that children lose their right to question, complain or seek justice. A healthy school must hold these principles together. There is a crucial distinction between authority and authoritarianism. Students respect teachers who are consistent, fair and willing to listen. 

They respect teachers who can admit mistakes and who correct behaviour without attacking the person. But students must also understand that respect is not optional. A classroom cannot function if every instruction becomes a negotiation. A school cannot function if every disciplinary decision is automatically interpreted as oppression. Teachers cannot teach effectively if they constantly fear that reasonable correction will be treated as hostility. The answer is not to weaken authority. 

The answer is to humanise it. It is tempting to place the entire responsibility on schools. That would be unfair. Children learn their attitudes towards authority not only from teachers, but also from family conversations, peers, digital media and the adults they observe. If children routinely hear contempt directed at teachers, institutions or anyone with whom adults disagree, they absorb more than the words. They absorb a model of conflict. Parents therefore have a critical role in building emotional discipline. 

Supporting a child does not mean automatically defending every action of that child. Questioning a school decision does not have to mean attacking the teacher. A healthier response is: “Tell me what happened. Let us understand it properly. If something wrong has happened, we will address it through the right channels.” That is how responsible citizenship is taught. A safe school cannot depend entirely on the temperament of individual teachers or students. It needs systems. Teachers need training in positive discipline, classroom management, child protection and emotional regulation. 

Students need explicit education about boundaries, respectful disagreement, conflict resolution and responsible digital behaviour. Parents need to understand the school’s expectations and grievance mechanisms. Teachers need safe and transparent channels through which concerns can be raised. School leaders must ensure that disciplinary procedures are predictable, proportionate and fair. The objective should never be to create a school where children are afraid of teachers. Nor should it be to create a school where teachers are afraid of children. 

The objective is to create an environment where everyone understands the boundaries within which dignity and learning can flourish. Perhaps the deeper question is what we mean by education. We measure examination results, university admissions, rankings and competitive achievements. These matter. But what happens when a highly educated young person cannot tolerate disagreement? What happens when a child can solve a difficult problem but cannot manage anger? What happens when a student can debate brilliantly but cannot accept being told “no”? These are educational failures too. The purpose of education is not simply to produce students who can answer questions. It is to develop human beings who can live responsibly with other human beings. 

Children must learn to disagree without degrading, complain without threatening, accept correction without feeling destroyed and exercise authority without abusing power. These are not peripheral life skills. They are essential to citizenship. The culture we create becomes the society we inherit. Schools are miniature societies. What we normalise within them eventually travels beyond their gates. If humiliation is normalised, children may learn to humiliate. If aggression is normalised, they may learn to retaliate. If authority is arbitrary, they may learn to distrust authority. 

If disagreement is treated as betrayal, they may become adults incapable of democratic dialogue. But if schools consistently model empathy, accountability, fairness and self-restraint, they teach something more valuable than any textbook: citizenship and humanity. These tragedies should therefore not become another cycle of public outrage that fades after a few days. They should provoke reflection among teachers, parents, school leaders, managements and students. We must ask whether our disciplinary practices are humane. Whether students understand the difference between disagreement and violence. 

Whether teachers feel protected and supported. Whether parents and schools are partners rather than adversaries. Above all, we must ask whether children are learning that every human being has dignity - and that neither power nor anger gives anyone the right to violate it. The school of the future cannot be built on fear. But neither can it be built on permissiveness. It must stand on something stronger: firm boundaries without cruelty, authority without arrogance, freedom without irresponsibility, correction without humiliation, and respect without fear. 

Education is ultimately not about producing children who simply know more. It is about helping them become people who can use what they know responsibly, compassionately and humanely. Perhaps the most important boundary our schools need to rebuild is the boundary between being powerful and abusing power, between being angry and becoming violent, and between demanding respect and learning to deserve it. That is the culture we owe our children ~ and one another.   

(The writer is head of department in a leading Kolkata school)

editorials.title: 10 years on, UPI has sent the bill
editorials.passage:
India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has entered its second decade by acquiring something it was designed to suppress: a transaction price. From October 15, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) will levy a 0.4 per cent Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on Person-to-Merchant (P2M) UPI payments above Rs 2,000, capped at Rs 300 for transactions of Rs 75,000 and above, with a flat Rs 5 charge for railways, telecom, insurance, and fuel. Consumers and every Person-to-Person (P2P) transfer, regardless of size, remain untouched. 

The announcement revives a decade-old argument: was India’s most celebrated public good ever truly free, and does charging for it now threaten the cashless economy it was meant to build? UPI’s first decade was extraordinary by any measure. Annual transactions rose from roughly 2 crore and worth Rs 0.07 lakh crore in FY17 to 24,162 crore worth Rs 314 lakh crore in FY26 – around 12,000-fold rise in volume and roughly 4,500-fold rise in value. The corresponding fall in average ticket size, from about Rs 3,900 to roughly Rs 1,300, shows UPI displacing small daily cash purchases as much as it enabled big-ticket digital ones. UPI now accounts for around 85 per cent of India’s digital-payment volume. Transactions above Rs 2,000 make up barely 4 per cent of merchant-payment volume but around two-thirds of its value - the statistical skew that lets NPCI claim 96 per cent of merchant transactions are unaffected. 

That is true, but it elides the difference between MDR’s statutory and its economic incidence: a merchant who formally bears the levy may still recover it through higher prices or thinner discounts. UPI’s first decade subsidised adoption; its second is monetising scale. UPI is free at the point of use, not free to operate. A parliamentary committee cited an industry estimate of Rs 20,700 crore in annual operating costs against a government allocation of just Rs 2,000 crore for FY27 – about a tenth of the cost. Banks and payment providers need revenue to fund capacity, cybersecurity, fraud prevention, and dispute resolution. 

In August 2026, PhonePe and Google Pay together processed 77.9 per cent of UPI volume and 81.6 per cent of value, monetising the relationship through lending and advertising while paying nothing for the rails beneath them – an asymmetry Parliament’s finance committee separately flagged. The Payments Council of India pressed for MDR’s return since the zero-MDR mandate began in January 2020, writing directly to the Prime Minister in March 2025. Read this way, the new framework looks less like a tax on citizens than a longdeferred settlement between the state and an industry it can no longer wholly subsidise. Will this push transactions to cash, and at what cost? 

India’s cash-to-GDP ratio has fallen from its pandemic peak of 14.4 per cent in FY21 to about 11 per cent in FY26, even as currency in circulation hit a record Rs 41.7 lakh crore, growing 11.9 per cent in FY26. But cash plumbing is already strained: ATM cash-management costs are projected to exceed Rs 20,000 crore annually, and intended cash-loading fell to 64 and 57 per cent of requirement in March and April 2026. An RBI study of UPI and cash demand finds that greater adoption is associated with lower cash demand nationally and across states, though the relationship is non-linear. The converse is a legitimate risk: if MDR redirects payments to cash, households and merchants may hold more currency outside banks. Deposits finance bank credit; currency outside banks does not. 

Persistent migration toward cash could weaken deposit mobilisation at the margin, prompting banks to raise deposit rates, compress margins or reprice loans – making credit marginally dearer, a risk policymakers must address rather than dismiss. The tax question is sharper still. UPI’s digital trail has been central to GST formalisation; cash is easier to omit from invoices and returns. An MDR nudging precisely the higher-ticket, revenue-relevant transactions back to cash would compound that risk, unlike the innocuous tea-stall payment officials cite. Consumption, too, may suffer: by restoring the friction UPI removed, the fee could lead to discretionary high-ticket spending being postponed. 

Two design flaws deserve scrutiny. First, structuring: splitting a Rs 10,000 bill into five Rs 2,000 transfers avoids the levy while multiplying the settlement and fraud-monitoring load MDR is meant to fund – self-defeating unless anti-structuring rules follow. Second, the P2P-P2M asymmetry: a Rs 1 lakh transfer to a friend stays free, while a Rs 2,001 transfer to a shopkeeper is charged, even though P2P transfers incur comparable infrastructure costs. NPCI’s implicit justification that merchants monetise the relationship elsewhere while individuals do not is not entirely defensible. 

The real test for this policy is not the MDR revenue collected, but that revenue net of the consumer-price pass-through, the cost of cash displaced onto a strained ATM network, and any tax leakage from transactions nudged back into currency. India built UPI to retire cash, not subsidise its comeback; financing the platform’s second decade should not mean pricing transactions back into the shadow economy it was designed to shrink. 

(The writer teaches Economics at IIM Ranchi. The views are personal.)’

editorials.title: Houthis’ power alters Red Sea dynamics
editorials.passage:
The Houthi movement , officially known as Ansar Allah (Supporters of God), has evolved from a localized Zaydi Shia revivalist group in northern Yemen into a formidable regional player capable of projecting power far beyond its borders. Originating in the 1990s as a theological movement against Saudi-backed Wahhabi influence and the perceived marginalisation by Yemen’s central government , the Houthis have leveraged years of civil war, strategic alliances, and geopolitical shifts to become a dominant force in the Middle East. Understanding the Houthis requires an examination of their core objectives and their significant potential for global and regional disruption. 

The Houthis' motivations operate on domestic, regional, and ideological levels. Consolidation of Domestic Rule: Domestically, the Houthis seek undisputed political and territorial control over Yemen. Since seizing the capital, Sana'a, in 2014 and successfully resisting a protracted military intervention by a Saudi-led coalition, they have positioned themselves as the de facto government of northern Yemen. Their internal goal is to formalise this governance, extract economic rents (such as port revenues and taxes), and dismantle any remaining domestic opposition. 

Regional Recognition and Ideological Legitimacy: The Houthis operate under a fierce anti-Western, anti-Zionist, and anti-imp erialist ideology, encapsulated in their official slogan: "God is the greatest, Death to America, Death to Israel, A Curse upon the Jews, Victory to Islam." They demand recognition as a sovereign and legitimate regional power rather than a mere rebel group or proxy. Integration into the ‘Axis of Resistance’: Over the past decade, the Houthis have deepened their alignment with Iran and its network of non-state allies, including Hezbollah in Lebanon and various militias in Iraq. 

While they retain local autonomy and are not absolute puppets of Tehran, they share Iran's strategic goal of countering American and Israeli influence in the Middle East. By actively participating in regional conflicts, they solidify their status within this alliance. The Houthis possess a disproportionate capacity to cause disruption, stemming primarily from Yemen’s unique geography and the group’s advanced asymmetric military capabilities. The most potent weapon in the Houthi arsenal is their geographical proximity to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a narrow chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Suez Canal. 

Through this corridor passes roughly 12 per cent of total global trade, including vast quantities of oil, liquefied natural gas, and consumer goods. By utilizing anti-ship cruise missiles, ballistic missiles, and sea drones, the Houthis have demonstrated that they can effectively hijack or disrupt commercial shipping. This forces global maritime firms to reroute vessels around the Cape of Good Hope, adding thousands of miles to journeys, delaying supply chains, inflating insurance premiums, and driving up global shipping costs. Transitioning from a guerrilla force into a technologically sophisticated military power, the Houthis possess long-range capabilities. 

They have launched drones and ballistic missiles targeting deep into Saudi Arabia (including vital Aramco oil facilities in the past), the United Arab Emirates, and southern Israel. The relatively low cost of Houthi drones compared to the millions of dollars required for state-sponsored air defence systems (like the US Patriot or Israel's Arrow systems) creates a highly asymmetric economic and military burden for their adversaries. Beyond shipping, the Houthis pose a latent threat to critical subsea infrastructure. The waters off the coast of Yemen host critical international submarine communication cables that carry a vast portion of the digital traffic between Asia, Europe, and the Middle East. 

Any disruption or sabotage directed at these cables carries the potential to cause massive telecommunications and financial disruption globally. The Houthis' disruptive potential also manifests internally. Their aggressive posture complicates international diplomatic efforts to secure a permanent peace legacy in Yemen. The diversion of shipping away from Houthi-controlled ports worsens what is already one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises, restricting the inflow of food, medicine, and international aid to millions of impoverished Yemenis. Ultimately, the Houthis have transformed from a localized northern Yemeni militia into a formidable geopolitical force capable of projecting power far beyond their borders. 

By leveraging asymmetric warfare, strategic regional alliances, and their geographic command over the Babal-Mandeb strait, they have effectively established a potent veto over global shipping lanes and regional stability. Their core objectives - consolidating internal governance, asserting zaydism-infused political dominance, and positioning themselves as a vanguard of anti-Western resistance - are structurally reinforced by this immense capacity for disruption. 

As the international community grapples with the fallout of clogged trade routes and shifting alliances, it is clear that the Houthis can no longer be viewed through a purely domestic lens. Any future framework for peace in the Middle East must confront the reality that their disruptive power has permanently altered the geopolitics of the Red Sea corridor. 

(The writer, a retired IFS officer, served as India’s Ambassador to Kuwait and Morocco and as ConsulGeneral in New York)

editorials.title: Beyond Jamui
editorials.passage:
The assault on two school students ~ a girl and a boy, both teenagers ~ in Bihar’s Jamui district is a test of more than policing. It challenges the social assumption that a young woman’s movements and associations are subject to scrutiny, and sometimes punishment, by men who appoint themselves guardians of morality. 

The violence against the girl and her male friend demands accountability, but the circumstances also expose a deeper struggle over personal freedom and dignity. The reported arrests, formation of a special investigation team and police action are necessary steps. Yet the case has also raised questions about how the authorities learned of the assault. The teenagers reportedly did not initially approach the police; investigators traced them after footage circulated online. 

This sequence deserves examination, without presuming that the victims’ silence reflects any failure. Shame, fear of exposure and concern about family or social consequences can complicate reporting, especially for minors. The circulation of the footage compounds the original violation. A recording intended to expose wrongdoing can become another instrument of humiliation when it reveals the identities of children. Action against accounts sharing the clips is therefore not a peripheral digital exercise. It is part of protecting the victims. 

The National Commission for Women’s intervention should reinforce the obligation to safeguard their privacy, rather than allow public outrage to turn into a second ordeal. The political response has been equally revealing. Describing such episodes as isolated incidents may be statistically defensible, but the phrase cannot substitute for evidence or answer public anxiety. Conversely, opposition leaders cannot establish a government’s overall failure through one disturbing case. Bihar’s record on women’s safety must be judged through credible data on violence, reporting, investigation, prosecution and conviction, alongside the accessibility of support for victims. 

The central issue, however, extends beyond party politics. If the assault arose from disapproval of two teenagers being together, it represents an attempt to enforce social conformity through intimidation. No private group has the authority to police another person’s relationships or movements. The state’s responsibility is to protect that freedom, not merely to punish its violent violation after the event. The reported arrest of suspects is a development, not the conclusion of the case. 

Investigators must establish each accused person’s role, preserve evidence and proceed through due process. Any alleged police encounter must also be subject to appropriate scrutiny; accountability cannot depend on the spectacle of force. Jamui should prompt more than expressions of shame or demands for exemplary punishment. It should lead to practical questions: Can minors report harassment safely? Are police equipped to respond sensitively? Are victims protected from exposure and intimidation? And can authorities demonstrate, through outcomes rather than assurances, that public spaces belong to girls as much as to boys? The measure of justice will not be the volume of outrage, but whether the teenagers regain their privacy and security ~ and whether the institutions responsible for protecting them learn from the assault.

editorials.title: Two-Front Reality
editorials.passage:
India’s strategic predicament in the Himalayas is increasingly shaped by the deepening partnership between China and Pakistan. The operationalisation of a joint boundary commission by Beijing and Islamabad, concerning territory claimed by India, underscores how developments involving one neighbour can affect New Delhi’s security calculations involving the other. The controversy stems from the 1963 Sino-Pakistan boundary agreement, under which Pakistan ceded the Shaksgam Valley to China. 

India rejects the arrangement, maintaining that the territory belongs to the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir and that Pakistan had no authority to transfer it. The renewed institutional engagement does not settle the dispute, but strengthens the administrative and diplomatic foundations of an arrangement India considers illegitimate. The distinction between legal claims and strategic realities is crucial. An agreement between two countries cannot extinguish a third country’s territorial claim. Yet sustained cooperation, infrastructure development and regularised border management can entrench disputed arrangements in practice. 

India must contend not merely with competing maps, but with the possibility that facts on the ground will become increasingly difficult to reverse. The timing carries geopolitical significance. India and China have sought to stabilise relations following years of military confrontation along the Line of Actual Control, particularly after the deadly Galwan clash of 2020. But engagement with Beijing has never guaranteed that China would moderate its partnership with Islamabad. The latest development illustrates the limits of treating bilateral normalisation as evidence of broader strategic accommodation. The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, linking western China with Pakistan’s Arabian Sea coast, adds an economic and infrastructural dimension to this relationship. 

Roads, transport networks and strategic facilities deepen interdependence while increasing the significance of the territory through which they pass. Cooperation consequently serves Beijing’s connectivity objectives as well as its wider regional interests. Nevertheless, India should resist interpreting every Chinese initiative as proof of an imminent coordinated military offensive. The boundary commission does not establish a new military situation along the LAC. Exaggerating its immediate implications could obscure the more consequential challenge: the consolidation of a partnership that complicates India’s security calculations across two frontiers. 

New Delhi’s response must extend beyond diplomatic protest. India needs sustained investment in border infrastructure, credible military preparedness and stronger diplomatic engagement with countries concerned about regional stability. It must also communicate its territorial position internationally with consistency, documentary evidence and persistence. Public declarations alone cannot counter the cumulative effects of another country’s institutional and infrastructural presence. The commission may not redraw the map today. But it reinforces a fundamental reality: India’s security challenges along its Chinese and Pakistani borders are closely interconnected, and its engagement with Beijing cannot be separated from the strategic implications of China’s partnership with Islamabad. New Delhi must prepare for this enduring complexity without confusing vigilance with the inevitability of conflict.

editorials.title: Colour codes
editorials.passage:
Jadavpur University’s convocation gown is saffron in colour. I remembered this when a friend, a Bengal-based scientist, shared a photo on social media, of herself on convocation day at JU, with comments on the aggression of a section of the right-wing ecosystem that has now singled out the university as its target — not merely through physical explosion on campus but through spurts of administrative and rhetorical bullying. My friend’s post reminded me that I too have a couple of photos, from the last year of the last millennium, of myself in the bright saffron robe, accepting my degree from the convocation guest, Karan Singh, the former governor of Jammu and Kashmir. But without all these photos, I don’t think I would have remembered the colour of the gown.

Back then, one could miss the colour. That was a Calcutta where saffron wasn’t loaded with a political ideology, even though the rise of Hindutva was well underway in other parts of India. Bengal’s political colour would remain red for another 10 years. In fact, politics in Bengal has been etched in colour for as long as I can remember. Redness marked communism everywhere, from graffiti to posters to the colour of your salaam . From the second decade of the 21st century, we entered the blue-and-white regime. Lacking the global force of the Communist Red, blue-and-white marked the personal preferences of the new leader, her desire to break free from decades of redness, and to mark the new aesthetic of a new political era.

Much throughout this history, for the Hindu Bengali sensibility, saffron managed to remain unworldly — the colour of renunciation and sacrifice. Even as it assumed political significance linked to right-wing, Hindutva outfits, particularly in northern and western India, in Bengal saffron continued to stand for other things. It stood, for instance, for genuine social service and educational excellence, with an understated composure that needed no political party to organise a march for gerua samman — the dignity of saffron. The most prominent articulation of the social and the educational mission of saffron has been the various Ramakrishna Mission institutions, which have spread worldwide but always with their nerve centre in Belur, and memories of modest origin in neighbourhoods and villages in Calcutta and Hooghly, from Dakhineswar and Shimla in North Calcutta to Kamarpukur and Joyrambati. Crucial centres of culture, hospitals and schools and colleges in Bengal bore the homespun texture of saffron with quiet grace. The Institute of Culture in Golpark continues to draw global dignitaries; the Seva Pratishthan hospital in South Calcutta continues to offer reliable and responsible medical care at affordable price in an age when healthcare of any quality is subject to corporate greed for profit. For large sections of the middle class, the schools have been synonymous with academic excellence and aspiration.

I spent a few years in one of these boarding schools run by saffron monks. Saffron, I learnt, was the colour that had to be attained after you had completed your white-robed years. White, the colour of brahmacharya , the period of youthful chastity, to give way to saffron, the colour of sannyas , the hue of the final renunciation of worldly attachments. For me, these shaped a deeply-loaded time, nestled in the strange intimacy of hymns and prayers and intense friendships and emotions and the peer-pressure around exams and the lure and the promise of successful secular careers in medicine and engineering, all contained within the pervasive umbrella of a saffron idyll and its pastoral care, shaded from the worldly turmoil of dusty streets, dysfunctional institutions and toxic politics — a world of paradoxes that went on to shape one of my books, The Scent of God.

Saffron stood not only for academic excellence but also promised a holistic bildung where spirituality guided the making of responsible secular citizens. It was a bildung that included fish, eggs and chicken in the boarding school fare that the monks consumed along with the students. I don’t know the particular inspiration behind the choice of saffron as the colour of the convocation gowns of Jadavpur University. But the imagination of saffron as a colour that united intellectual aspiration with spiritual discipline and social responsibility was so entrenched in wide segments of the Bengali mind that the colour evoked peace and promise at the same time. If I didn’t notice the saffron of the gowns we wore that day at the JU convocation, it was because of the entrenchment of the colour in our collective sensibility made it a natural colour in an academic environment. Its spiritual texture might occasionally be a troubling presence in a Left-leaning intellectual landscape. But even with such frictions, a saffron hue in an academic space was a natural thing.

The saffron enshrined in our hearts, notwithstanding the left-secular sarcasm that occasionally caressed it, could never become the colour of hooliganism. It imposed restrictions neither on diet nor on faith, following the tradition of its founding figures — Shri Ramakrishna, Ma Sarada, Swami Vivekananda. Neither its deep academic commitment nor its capacious spiritual character could imagine a ritual ‘cleansing’ of the room of an academic administrator of another faith after she had been forced to leave the institution — as has recently happened in a college in central Calcutta. This was the saffron we wore, with submerged respect, while receiving our degrees at Jadavpur University.

Will the saffron of sanatan dharma take over the festival most deeply cherished by the Bengali? But Bengal is nothing if not nuanced with paradoxes. Pujo in Bengal has always evoked Basanti rather than Saffron — the mustard yellow of the spring ritual whose untimely invocation in autumn by Lord Rama shapes the autumnal sharadiya . The neo- sanatani mandate to replace sharadiya by Durga Puja is also the dismissal of an earthy, seasonal festival for a narrow and austere religious ritual. Will the homely daughter clad in the name and the colour of Basanti pay a visit to the house of sanatani saffron?

Saikat Majumdar’s most recent book is Open Intelligence: Education Between Art and Artificial

editorials.title: Prestige over precious lives
editorials.passage:
September marks a global bid to prevent suicide. Indian Institutes of Technology report the highest number of student deaths by suicide among Centrally-funded institutions in India, indicating a concentrated and escalating crisis within the IIT system. Around 160 student deaths by suicide were reported in the past two decades at IITs. The Global IIT-IIM Alumni Support Group documented 65 student deaths by suicide across 23 IITs between 2021 and 2025. In August 2026, following the eighth death by suicide in just 30 months at IIT Delhi, students protested over five consecutive days with placards that read “IIT admin sharm karo ”, demanding an independent investigation, accountability from the administration, resignation of the deans of student affairs, and one crore in compensation for the victim’s family. IIT Delhi faced a campus deadlock; the director issued warnings of disciplinary action while the administration reconstituted an inquiry panel headed by a retired high court judge.

Protests of this scale are rare at IITs because of the fear of strict punishment and campus surveillance. The fear was in the air during the protests as students spoke to the media with their backs turned away from the recording lenses for fear of administrative retribution. A student pressed the point to a newspaper journalist: “Undergraduates in their final year fear placement debarment, PhD scholars risk having their thesis submissions and degrees stalled for years… Everyone enters IIT with high hopes. It is a dream. But after becoming a student here, those dreams are shattered… every single day, we find ourselves in the midst of more stress.” These developments, coupled with recurrent instances of denial of natural justice, underscore the fact that the administration’s fulcrum operates to protect the prestige of the IITs even when lives are lost, pointing to an extraordinary moral failure at enormously publicly-funded institutes of national importance.

In 2025, the Supreme Court came down heavily on IIT Delhi for evading the duty to lodge a first information report even though the parents alleged caste discrimination as the reason for their son’s death by suicide, which was dismissed as a case of academic pressure. The top court remarked that an institution cannot bypass procedures established by law “just because something happened in the hostel of an eminent educational institution like IIT-Delhi”. Cognisant of the recurrent institutional apathy, the top court constituted a 10-member National Task Force for Student Mental Health and Suicide Prevention, endowing it with judicial powers. The apex court has found inordinate delays in filing FIRs following deaths by suicide of students at IITs. It issued a stern warning to 17 IITs for not participating in the suicide survey conducted by the NTFSMHSP despite multiple reminders. In January 2026, based on the interim report submitted by the latter, the court ordered that campus deaths by suicide be reported to the local police without fail.

According to Marshall Ganz, a professor at Harvard University, stories consist of three elements: Story of Self, Story of Us, and Story of Now. An individual grievance may not always be about that individual in itself and may represent collective suffering. An empathetic response to a story helps take preventive action to de-escalate suffering that stems from structural violence and apathy. Stories are worth telling and listening to for they reveal the complexities of lived realities, kindling new imaginations about interventions couched in compassion and an ethic of care. Stories evoke feelings of pain, guilt, and helplessness, allowing us to be compassionate and empathetic toward others and ourselves. The unending quest by IITs to tell a single story of prestige is a symptom of institutional exceptionalism that pays scant attention to individual dignity, diverse lived experiences or life itself.

As the African writer, Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, puts it, “Stories matter. Many stories matter. Stories have been used to dispossess and to malign. Stories can be used to empower and to humanise. Stories can break the dignity of a people, but stories can also repair that broken dignity.” Richard Kearney, the author of On Stories , reminds us that “An unnarrated life is not worth living.” Stories offer a public language for experiences we never speak about due to fear, shame, or social ridicule. Thus, they offer recognition to profound emotional landscapes that are trained to silence. Stories help process trauma by turning chaotic and painful experiences into structured narratives. In fact, the World Health Organization has recognised the power of storytelling in achieving public health outcomes.

Dismissing a complaint and violating procedures established by law to protect the prestige of the IIT are forms of moral violence. Only an organisational model based on compassion can grant ‘permission to narrate’ stories that are antithetical to institutional prestige. These tales would enable the creation of transformative strategies for healing and systems change. IITs should listen to stories because listening is compassion; listening is mental health care.

Sudarshan R. Kottai is Assistant Professor, Department of Humanities and Social Sciences, IIT Palakkad

editorials.title: A bombshell: Editorial on dissent within the EC and erosion of electoral credibility
editorials.passage:
Public anxiety with and criticism of the Election Commission of India had been gaining ground ever since the contentious Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls gathered pace across the country. The exercise has been deemed exclusionary — not without reason. Matters have even reached India’s highest court on this issue. It appears that voices of concern had been raised within the EC itself. The news of such an unprecedented rupture within the institution is now in the public domain after a report — a razor-sharp and rare feat of journalism — in The Indian Express revealed that two election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had objected — on record — to several measures taken by India’s apex poll regulatory body as many as 14 times in the last 10 months.

The concerns of Mr Sandhu and Mr Joshi merit serious examination. They pertain to crucial aspects such as voters’ rights, the fairness of the SIR and, crucially, the concentration of power within the EC. For instance, Mr Joshi had warned that a fresh stipulation for Form 6 — a new voter is now asked whether his or her name and those of his or her parents feature in the electoral roll of the last SIR — was unwarranted. Mr Joshi had also expressed reservation regarding the centralisation of the electoral database, essentially dismantling the EC’s assurance that the preparation of electoral rolls is autonomous by design. That is not all. The EC informed the Supreme Court that in Bengal — the SIR was perhaps the most contested in this state — over 16 lakh appeals had been filed seeking the deletion of names included by judicial officers. Mr Sandhu, quite rightly, raised the point of the EC appealing against the inclusion of names of voters who had passed the scrutiny of authorities appointed on the ground. The disenfranchisement of potential voters in Goa had been attributed to a software issue: the EC has responded by stating that its digital platforms subscribe to data security protocols. Despite all this, the two conscientious commissioners went unheard institutionally. Even a knock on the cabinet secretary’s door did not yield the desired result. Significantly, the red flags cited by Mr Sandhu and Mr Joshi cannot be consigned to the bin. The law is clear that while the CEC may be the first among equals, the EC’s transactions must, when differences crop up among the commissioners, adhere to the principle of majority.

The political fallouts of this exposé have been unsurprising. The Opposition, which has been expressing its doubts regarding the CEC’s integrity, is claiming that it stands vindicated. But the crisis points to a deeper challenge. The EC is an august institution. But its majesty is contingent upon it being, like Caesar’s wife, above suspicion. It is quite clear that the CEC has not been able to adhere to the standards expected of him. But this is more than an individual failure. The prospect of erosion in the EC was first raised when the Centre amended the rules of appointment to that office in a bid to tighten its grip on the office holders. A two-judge bench of the Supreme Court has ordered that the issue be placed before the chief justice of India for the creation of a Constitution bench. But it cannot be denied that the EC and, by that logic, the entire electoral — democratic — process has been brought into question.

editorials.title: Chinks in the armour
editorials.passage:
The paid advertisements on Instagram promoting child sexual abuse material in India represent one of the gravest failures of platform governance. Unlike user-generated posts that may escape detection, these advertisements passed through Meta’s own advertising infrastructure, appeared on user feeds, and directed users towards encrypted Telegram channels. Following a BBC investigation, the ministry of electronics and information technology issued a notice to Meta seeking an explanation.

Meta has consistently maintained that it employs multiple safeguards against online child sexual exploitation content that range from automated machine learning classifiers and hash-matching technologies such as PhotoDNA to large-scale, human-led content moderation. PhotoDNA compares an uploaded image against databases containing digital hashes of previously identified CSAM. In case of an existing match, the content is automatically flagged and removed. However, the technology cannot detect newly created CSAM or encrypted material.

Facebook also employs teams of human content moderators and reviewers to determine whether the content violates Meta’s Community Standards and whether the image should be reported as CSAM. Reports have suggested that moderators may rely on Tanner Scale, a tool used by forensic scientists and medical professionals to estimate the puberty stage in an individual, to estimate the age of the humans in a particular image during their review. This approach has been criticised because puberty stages do not reliably correspond with chronological age and fail to account for variations across populations.

With the emergence of AI-generated CSAM, the limitations of existing detection technologies have become pronounced. Unlike traditional CSAM, AI-generated material may depict real children, fictitious children, digitally de-aged adults, or entirely synthetic subjects. Conventional hash-matching technologies offer little protection against these. Open-source models present an even greater challenge because they may be modified offline and trained exclusively on CSAM datasets, making regulatory oversight significantly difficult. Specific applications are popularly used to nudify images of clothed children. Given their easy availability, the United Kingdom is considering a blanket ban on these. At times, chatbots also hallucinate, generating sexual contents on a regular and non-sexual user prompt. Furthermore, a report by the Internet Watch Foundation has also claimed that users of the dark web regularly engage in exchanging and sharing of CSAM databases.

While there is no specific mention of CSAM in the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, the law has sections that criminalise a range of offences involving sexual exploitation of children. POCSO rules also require intermediaries such as Facebook and Instagram to report any circulation of child pornography. Additionally, Section 67B of the Information Technology Act, 2000 punishes publication or transmission of CSAM while Section 79 complements such protections by regulating intermediaries and third-party content hosted on such platforms. The due diligence obligations on the intermediaries are further elaborated in the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.

The Instagram CSAM advertisement issue should not be viewed as a failure of content moderation. When intermediaries actively review, monetise and algorithmically distribute paid advertisements, they occupy a role that extends beyond passive hosting. India’s intermediary liability framework should evolve to address platform-controlled advertising systems and emerging AI-generated child sexual abuse material.

Anmol Ratan and Priya Chaudhary are lawyers and researchers

editorials.title: Fill the gaps: Editorial on Bengal's zero-enrolment schools and public education crisis
editorials.passage:
The Bengal government is considering repurposing 933 government-aided schools with zero enrolment for other public uses. Bengal has 4,133 zero-enrolment schools, nearly half the national total, according to the latest UDISE+ data. Demographic changes cannot fully explain why functioning schools have failed to attract pupils. Parents perceive — justifiably — that public schools are poorly run, under-supervised, and have staff focused more on bureaucratic duties such as electoral and census responsibilities than teaching. In urban areas, parents increasingly prefer private, English-medium institutions, which are thought to offer better prospects in education. Besides poor infrastructure and inconvenient locations, UDISE+ analysis also suggests that the documentation for admission makes enrolment difficult for scheduled tribes and other backward groups. Repurposing schools without investigating these causes would accelerate the decline in education in the state.

Each zero-enrolment school should first undergo an independent assessment of local demand and its capacity for revival. Viable institutions should be regenerated through English-medium sections, better infrastructure, transport facilities, simpler admission procedures and sustained enrolment campaigns. Local bodies should identify out-of-school children and consult communities about what would persuade students to return. Public-private partnerships could provide academic expertise, management support and investment where the State lacks capacity provided public ownership, affordable access and government oversight are preserved. The government’s priority must be to restore public education.

editorials.title: When technology stops serving humanity
editorials.passage:
As the world watches the landmark $18 billion settlement against Meta unfold in California, something larger than a dispute over Facebook and Instagram is taking shape. The case, which began on August 18, has been brought by attorneys general from 29 US states, alleging that Meta deliberately designed its platforms to be addictive to children, concealed evidence of harm and violated laws protecting children’s privacy. The States are seeking not merely compensation but fundamental changes to how social media operates its platforms, including restrictions on age, algorithms and features such as infinite scrolling.

What makes the case particularly significant is not simply the number of states involved. It is the fact that the state itself has become the plaintiff. This is not an individual claiming that social media harmed him or her. It is government asserting that a technology company’s business model can create a social harm serious enough to warrant collective state intervention. And this is not happening in isolation. US governments, along with many others, have increasingly begun to treat artificial intelligence itself as a matter of national security and public policy.

Why this sudden awakening? The obvious explanations are familiar. There are concerns about children, misinformation, privacy, job displacement, cybersecurity, national security and the more dramatic doomsday scenarios surrounding artificial intelligence. However, the deeper issue is more fundamental: what do we expect technology to do for humanity?

There is no single definition of technology. Nonetheless, one could zero in on an intuitive definition: technology is the practical application of human knowledge, ideas, and skills to create tools, machines, and systems that solve problems, make work more efficient, and improve human life. Two common elements deserve attention: first, technology solves problems, and second, it improves the quality of human life. Think of any technology, and it will satisfy both. Medical technologies seek to diagnose, prevent or cure disease. The automobile allows people to travel faster and farther. Computers automate calculations and processes that would otherwise consume enormous amounts of human time.

Artificial intelligence, as a technology, compromises these two basic principles. AI are not meant to solve any problem from first principles, but rather to automate or expedite an existing solution. It can seemingly curate a solution that already exists in human knowledge. Therefore, fundamentally, AI, despite its extraordinary value, does not necessarily extend the frontier of human knowledge in the way revolutionary technologies are traditionally expected to do. Its immense value lies in its ability to compress, organise, synthesise and accelerate the vast stock of knowledge that humanity has already accumulated, turning existing knowledge into usable solutions at unprecedented speed and scale.

For example, AI can give you a survey of the state-of-the-art solutions available to tackle the greenhouse effect or control wildfires raging in many parts of the globe. However, it cannot produce an innovative solution to these problems that is unknown to mankind. Second, and most ironically, AI violates the second premise of technology by eliminating humans from the process itself. Putting robots with agentic AI in manufacturing takes both the labourers and managers out of the factory. AI in professional services is not primarily designed to improve the productivity of lawyers, accountants, analysts or programmers; its commercial attraction lies precisely in reducing the need for them. AI is therefore designed to replace humans for profit, making a handful of humans super rich.

This raises an uncomfortable question. If technology progressively removes humans from production, decision-making, creativity and even social interaction, at what point does technological progress begin to undermine the very human welfare it was supposed to enhance?

Extend the logic a little further, and it is not difficult to imagine that such unabated development would compromise the State’s interests as well. Therefore, the State’s recent awakening to the perils of AI industries probably reflects those concerns, triggered by recent cybersecurity threats.

Further, AI can diffuse rapidly through software, cloud computing and open models. Its proliferation is consequently much harder to contain. A teenager can access a powerful AI model. A company can deploy an agent. A foreign actor can distribute a model globally. The barrier to entry is dramatically lower. The State therefore faces a dilemma. It has historically encouraged technological competition on the assumption that superior technology ultimately produces superior outcomes for society. Therefore, the race for increasingly powerful AI may contain a paradox: the more successful the race becomes, the more it may undermine the human role that gives the technology its social purpose.

A historical parallel is nuclear technology. During the Cold War, technological competition initially encouraged states to build increasingly destructive arsenals. Eventually, however, States recognised that no one could meaningfully win an unlimited nuclear race. The logic of technological superiority had become self-defeating. Regulation, arms control and non-proliferation followed. AI is obviously not nuclear technology, and the comparison should not be overstated. But the underlying logic is relevant. A technology race can become socially destructive when the private incentive to develop greater capability diverges from the collective interest in controlling its consequences. The Meta case may therefore be more important than it first appears. It is part of a broader transition from a world in which governments largely asked, “How quickly can technology grow?” to one in which they increasingly ask, “What kind of technology should society allow to grow?”

The ultimate issue is not whether AI should be stopped. It will not be. The issue is whether society can impose a threshold beyond which technological capability must be judged not by how powerful the machine becomes, but by whether it continues to serve human beings. The state is beginning to recognise that technology cannot be allowed to define its own social purpose. Markets can decide what is profitable. They cannot, by themselves, decide what is good for humanity. That responsibility ultimately belongs to society and therefore to the state.

Therefore, one useful guiding principle for addressing the peril of this dystopian technology is to restore these two values. In this context, the Pro-Human AI Declaration, organised by the Future of Life Institute in March 2026, offers a timely guiding principle by emphasising five principles: keeping humans in control, preventing the concentration of power, protecting the human experience, preserving human agency and liberty, and ensuring responsibility and accountability for AI companies

Published on September 24, 2026

editorials.title: Cyber resilience in banking sector
editorials.passage:
Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled cyberattacks have emerged as the leading perceived cybersecurity risk over the next year, according to the RBI’s recent Financial Stability Report. Agentic models like Claude’s Mythos series can autonomously expose vulnerabilities in a financial institution’s infrastructure that might otherwise go undiscovered. These models reduce the time and skill required by an attacker, thereby making cyberattacks more scalable and potent.

The potential for misuse has already led to access restrictions through US government directives and deliberate restrictions by frontier AI providers. It is reasonable to speculate that such restrictions are temporary, with many restrictions already rescinded and models being launched in the public domain. It is only a matter of time before many more actors, including bad actors, gain access to such capabilities.

In this context, this piece examines how AI is reshaping the cyber risk landscape in the banking sector.

The banking sector is one of the most frequent targets for cyberattacks. Neither the RBI nor the financial institutions are new to managing cyber risk. What triggers alarm bells about Mythos-like models is the possibility that the financial infrastructure is under-defended and the scale at which harm could materialise if vulnerabilities are exploited. Not only are the likelihood and severity of a cyberattack unknown, but there is also uncertainty about whether cyber defences that have worked till now will hold up against emerging threats.

AI-enabled cyber risks are heightened for financial institutions as they are embedded within a deeply interconnected ecosystem of fintechs, technology providers and other third parties, extending the attack surface beyond their own walls. The 2024 ransomware attack on C Edge Technologies, a core technology service provider, temporarily disrupted payment systems across 300 cooperative and rural banks, leaving customers unable to withdraw cash at ATMs or use UPI. This interconnectedness magnifies the asymmetry between the attackers and the defending financial institutions. An attacker may need to find just one vulnerability in shared infrastructure to cause significant harm, while the bank must defend against every one of them.

Financial institutions have limited control over when, where, and how an AI-enabled cyberattack will occur. Therefore, to minimise the severity and consequences of harm, the focus must extend beyond anticipating every attack to ensuring they can withstand and recover from one. A resilience-based approach in cybersecurity recognises this uncertainty as an integral part of decision-making, thereby making it less unsettling. It expects defenders to learn from real-world data and recalibrate their responses through monitoring and feedback.

If one were to stress test institutional resilience against AI-enabled cyber risks, the RBI’s FREE AI Committee Report found that only one-fourth of respondents had formal processes in place to mitigate AI-related incidents or failures. Of the 127 entities that reported use of AI, only 14 per cent conducted regular audits, only 18 per cent maintained audit logs and 14 per cent conducted real-time performance monitoring. By that measure, the answer to building the banking sector’s cyber resilience today cannot rest on individual institutions only.

No single institution will have the visibility, data or capability to anticipate and prepare for every unknown threat. This is coupled with considerable variation across banks, NBFCs, and microfinance institutions in terms of technological maturity, operational capacity and financial resources.

The RBI has already begun to respond to risks arising from agentic and frontier AI models. For instance, the recent Draft Guidance on Model Risk Management requires banks to safeguard models against cyber risks. The recent Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework Directions, 2026 require financial institutions to dynamically incorporate lessons learnt from past incidents, tests and drills to improve response plans. However, regulatory expectations from financial institutions alone may not suffice. This is where ecosystem-level solutions become important and drawing on emerging developments, the following interventions could help build cyber resilience across the financial sector.

First, operationalise real-time information sharing among financial institutions in coordination with the Computer Security Incident Response Team- Financial Sector (CSIRT-Fin). Sharing information on cyberattacks, near-misses or incidents involving non-financial partners, such as technology providers, would give all institutions timely intelligence to anticipate and prepare for a similar threat. Such a mechanism is more likely to work if reporting is non-punitive, a practice commonly followed in aviation. For instance, the NASA Aviation Safety Reporting System encourages pilots, maintenance technicians, air traffic controllers and others to report unsafe occurrences, close calls and hazardous situations by making such reporting confidential.

Second, use intelligence generated from this mechanism to develop a catalogue of AI-enabled cyber risk scenarios and plausible mitigation strategies that financial institutions can use to stress test their systems against. Such a catalogue can be an equaliser, particularly for smaller institutions. It would give financial institutions a view of priority risks, including those initially identified by only one or two institutions. It can provide a common understanding of the risk, the attack vector, potential impact and possible responses for containment, if the risk materialises. One such library of cyber scenarios is maintained by the UK Cross Market Operational Resilience Group, which has recently added scenarios of threat actors using agentic and generative AI to create false employee and customer accounts.

Lastly, set a baseline of resilience standards against AI-enabled cyber risks for all institutions across the banking, securities, pensions and insurance sector, irrespective of size, geographical presence, IT set-up or the perceived risk profile. Advancements in AI-enabled cyber offensive strategies are challenging the principle of proportionality in cybersecurity. Digital conversations, shared drives, emails, for instance, may appear less risky but can be the attack vector exploited, precisely because it is subject to weaker oversight. The Inter-Ministerial Group on the Financial Sector Cybersecurity Strategy, mandated by the Financial Stability and Development Council last year to develop a unified cybersecurity strategy, should use this opportunity to establish this baseline of non-negotiable standards.

As AI’s offensive capabilities make cyberattacks cheaper, more pervasive and harder to anticipate, getting the fundamentals of cyber hygiene right is more important than ever. But the scale and speed of the emerging risk demand more than what a financial institution can do alone. The RBI’s priority should be to raise the baseline of sectoral resilience through ecosystem-level solutions that help institutions learn from collective intelligence, anticipate emerging risks and prepare before they become a crisis.

The writer is Research Associate, Dvara Research

Published on September 24, 2026

editorials.title: Effect of a wider EPFO net
editorials.passage:
The Cabinet raised the mandatory wage ceiling for coverage under the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation from ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 a month on September 16, 2026, effective the next day. The government expects the change to add more than 51 lakh workers to mandatory provident fund, pension and insurance cover, the first revision to the ceiling since September 2014. Read as a policy output, that number is real. Read as a policy outcome for India’s labour market, it measures something else entirely: how many people already in salaried jobs are now formally registered, not how many new salaried jobs exist.

The timing was not entirely the government’s choice. The Supreme Court, hearing a public interest litigation on the stagnant ceiling, directed the Centre and EPFO on January 5, 2026 to decide on a revision within four months. A Bench of Justices JK Maheshwari and Atul S Chandurkar noted that the ₹15,000 limit, unchanged since 2014, had left workers earning above the State and Central minimum wage outside EPFO’s reach altogether. The Cabinet acted more than four months after that court-set deadline had passed.

The new ceiling also sits close to what a typical salaried worker already earns. Average monthly earnings for men in regular wage or salaried employment stood at ₹24,217 in 2025, according to the National Statistics Office’s Periodic Labour Force Survey Annual Report. For women in the same category, average earnings were ₹18,353. Both figures fall inside the ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 band, the exact segment the Cabinet says will now come under compulsory coverage. This means the expansion largely captures workers who were already earning close to, or above, the old ceiling, not workers moving into new kinds of formal work. A worker hired last month at ₹20,000 a month was legally outside mandatory EPF coverage. From September 17, the same wage brings automatic enrolment. The job has not changed. Only its treatment under the law has.

Measured against its own history, the ceiling rose 66.7 per cent in nominal terms. Annualised over the 12 years it stayed frozen, that works out to close to 4.3 per cent a year, below the 5.8 per cent and 7.2 per cent nominal wage growth recorded for male and female regular salaried workers between 2024 and 2025 alone. The ceiling has caught up with wages accumulated since 2014. It has not overtaken the pace at which those wages are currently rising.

The Cabinet’s own note described the measure as one that would give “further impetus to formalisation of employment, worker retention and long-term retirement security.” The estimated annual government outgo is ₹11,339 crore, against existing budgetary support of ₹10,250 crore, and ₹56,696 crore over five years. That is public money spent on retirement security for workers who already hold salaried jobs. It does not answer a separate question: whether India is creating enough new regular jobs to begin with.

That question has a clearer, less encouraging answer. Regular wage or salaried employment accounted for 23.6 per cent of India’s workforce in 2025, up from 22.4 per cent in 2024, per the same PLFS report. Self-employment remained the largest category, at 56.2 per cent of workers, most of it outside any employer-employee relationship and therefore outside EPFO’s reach. The share of workers with a formal salary slip grew by little more than one percentage point in a year. EPFO already administers funds for 7.98 crore contributing members across 7.68 lakh establishments, one of the largest social security systems in the world. The 51 lakh addition, by comparison, is a single rule change applied to a base already inside the formal wage economy.

In evaluation terms, EPFO enrolment is an output indicator. It counts an administrative event, a person added to a scheme. It is not an outcome indicator for the labour market, which would require counting new jobs, not old jobs newly registered. India has few high-frequency outcome indicators for salaried employment, which is precisely why an output indicator like EPFO membership gets read as a proxy for job creation. The two are not interchangeable.

Unemployment data sharpen the point. India’s overall unemployment rate eased to 5 per cent in August 2026, a six-month low, according to the NSO’s Periodic Labour Force Survey monthly bulletin, which measures activity over the seven days preceding the survey. Urban unemployment, measured on the same basis, held at 6.8 per cent, roughly unchanged from July. Cities, where regular salaried jobs concentrate, continue to show the weakest labour absorption in the country. A wider EPFO net changes little for a worker who cannot find a job to be enrolled into.

India’s formalisation story, on this evidence, is an output story before it is an outcome story: deeper protection for jobs that already exist, not more of the regular jobs a growing labour force needs. The EPFO ceiling now covers most of what a salaried worker earns. It says nothing about how many more salaried workers the economy is producing.

The writer is an independent public policy consultant

Published on September 24, 2026

editorials.title: Tech teams take a new shape
editorials.passage: By Mritunjay Singh Most people want to know whether AI will replace engineers. Wrong question, and it produces the wrong planning. AI is not thinning teams evenly – it is changing their shape. The organisation charts that most of us grew up with – a broad, stable middle of people who coordinate, translate, review, and pass work along – is quietly compressing.
