What is left is an hourglass: deep domain experts at the top, AI-augmented execution at the bottom, and a much narrower band in between. I will not say this as a prediction, but as something we are already managing. Where the value moved For thirty years, a lot of engineering value lived in the middle. There was a person who would take the senior architect's intent and turn it into something a delivery team could act on, a reviewer who caught the defect before it shipped, and the coordinator who kept the moving parts in sync.That work was real and valuable, because translation between “what we want” and “what got built” was expensive. AI has made a large part of that translation cheap. A capable engineer with the right tools now does work that used to require a whole chain of people. The distance between an idea and a working prototype has collapsed, and the roles that existed to manage the distance compressed. ALSO READ Again, when a small team can produce in days what used to take a quarter, managing that team stops being about pacing handoffs.  It is now about keeping a much faster loop coherent – deciding, correcting, and re-aiming – while the work is still in motion. Speed does not just compress the middle, but changes what managing a team stands for. What we are experiencing is not an “AI takes jobs,” position, but how it fills the space between jobs. The two ends get more valuable, not less The new hourglass, however, does not shrink the whole team. It makes the two ends more important. At the top, domain expertise becomes the scarcest asset. AI can generate a hundred plausible options but cannot tell you which one is right for a medical device that has to pass regulatory approval, or a vehicle platform that must survive fifteen years of the real world. Judgment rooted in decades of context is the thing AI most conspicuously lacks. At the bottom, execution accelerates. An engineer early in their career, paired with AI, now ships things that would have taken a team a few years ago. The fresher paradox For years, the entry point into engineering was the routine work across first drafts, test cases, and boilerplates. AI now does a lot of that. The bar to enter has gone up, not down, because the apprenticeship tasks are now the first ones automated. And the fix – changing what we expect a fresher to arrive knowing – more domain grounding, more comfort orchestrating AI rather than competing with it. That is on us, not on a twenty-two-year-old. What this means if you run a team Three things I would tell any operating leader today. First, stop planning headcount as a single number. Plan the shape. The question is no longer “how many engineers,” but “how deep is our expert bench, how strong is our AI-augmented execution layer, and what is genuinely left in the middle.” Those are three different hiring and reskilling problems. Second, invest in the middle band you keep. The coordination that remains is higher-order, orchestrating human and AI work together – a real skill and a scarce one. Move your best middle-layer people toward that, deliberately. Third, be honest with your people. The worst thing a leader can do right now is issue reassuring statements that everyone knows are not quite true. Tell them the shape is changing and where the value is going. People can handle a hard truth with a plan, not a comfortable message followed by an unpleasant surprise. The part I will not oversell AI is changing the shape of engineering teams. It is not, in my experience, replacing the need for engineers who understand the physical, regulated, unforgiving domains we work in. If anything, it is raising the premium on them. The hourglass is not about a smaller team, but a differently shaped one. And the organisations that plan for the shape, rather than argue about the headline, are the ones that will come out ready for tomorrow. The writer is chief operating officer, L&T Technology Services.Disclaimer: The views expressed are the author’s own and do not reflect the official policy or position of Financial Express.

editorials.title: Abandoned, dismissed and gaslighted: there is no excuse for the way ME sufferers have been betrayed
editorials.passage:
I ’ve spent my working life covering neglected issues. But few are neglected like the devastating chronic condition ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis, or chronic fatigue syndrome). In severe cases, the illness shuts down people’s lives almost entirely, causing an extreme loss of energy and a wide range of physical and cognitive symptoms that can prevent patients from working, socialising and, sometimes, even moving or eating. Yet these people have been more or less airbrushed from our minds.

To find out what this neglect looks like in practice, this week I put out a call on Bluesky asking people with ME/CFS about their recent experiences of treatment. I was immediately inundated with horrifying testimonies. “I’ve just been completely abandoned”; “a 10-year waiting list for treatment”; “we’ve given up seeking medical support”; “stuck in limbo”; “I just felt utterly unheard, invalidated”. I’ve been sent hundreds of shocking and heart-rending accounts.

Exact numbers are hard to establish, but in the UK alone, an estimated 400,000 people live with the condition. It affects women far more than men , by a ratio of about 4:1, according to a study in England. The number of people with long Covid, some of whom meet the diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS, was estimated in 2024 at 2 million in England and Scotland.

You might have imagined politicians and the media would be all over it. Instead, this great social crisis is met with silence or worse. Some outlets, despite the overwhelming weight of evidence, have mocked or trivialised these conditions.

There’s a long, dark history here , rooted in centuries of dismissal of predominantly female illnesses as “hysterical”, and amplified in recent decades by government attempts to reduce the benefits bill and insurers’ attempts to reduce payouts. If you can establish that a condition is caused by malingering, poor self-care or a negative attitude, you won’t have to cough up.

Official guidance in many countries was informed by a series of deeply flawed studies that purported to show these illnesses could be treated with cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), or graded exercise therapy (GET). In 2020, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) found that the quality of all the research promoting these therapies as curative treatments for ME/CFS was either “low” or, in most cases, “very low”. In 2021, it stopped recommending these therapies as primary treatments. We now know CBT cannot treat the condition (though it can sometimes help patients to come to terms with it), while GET is not only useless but actively dangerous, as exercise can trigger one of the most devastating ME/CFS symptoms: post-exertional malaise (PEM). PEM robs people of their remaining energy, rendering many patients bedbound, sometimes incapable of almost all movement.

Since then, two other things have happened. At the inquest into the death of a young ME/CFS patient, the coroner ruled that provision in the health service for patients with severe ME “was and is nonexistent”. Something would have to be done. And a number of seeming scientific breakthroughs , some very recent , have begun inching towards identifying possible biological causes of both ME/CFS and long Covid. Now, or so we should hope, it’s undeniable.

So what has changed as a result of these shifts? Alongside the horror and heartbreak in the testimonies of the people who emailed me, I was struck by the sense of sheer relief that someone, anyone, was asking the question.

Many said they are still being treated as if they have a psychological illness, and still being pushed into GET and CBT. One patient told me: “I’ve gone from relatively mild to now mostly house- and bedbound, largely thanks to repeated attempts at graded exercise and ‘pushing through’.” A few days ago, an NHS clinic told another patient to undertake “graded exercise” and “simply to walk, despite the fact I’m a wheelchair user”.

One mother told me “the consultant cardiologist recommended a graded exercise programme” and “a treadmill test” for her bedbound son. When she told him this contradicted Nice guidelines, he replied: “Well, what do you want me to do?” Another made the same challenge to her GP, but the doctor “denied this strongly and reiterated to my daughter that she should do the exercises”. This is very common: many doctors, I’m told, seem unaware of the new guidelines and react defensively when challenged. In many practices, GET has simply been rebranded as “building tolerance” or “pacing up” or “a little more activity each day”.

Patients report being treated with “contempt and derision”. Loads are still being offered CBT. Some have been propelled by NHS doctors towards quack private “cures”, now offered by a growing industry that preys on people’s desperation.

Others tell me they’ve not been pushed into inappropriate treatments, but “that’s only because I receive no treatment for it whatsoever”. Some have had to explain to their doctors what ME/CFS is. And it gets worse. I’ve been contacted by parents who have been accused of fabricating and inducing illness and even referred to social services, because doctors who seem to know nothing about ME/CFS believe they are making up their children’s symptoms.

It’s as if nothing has been learned. Perhaps that’s not surprising. A freedom of information request to NHS England found that, of the tens of thousands of practitioners who would benefit from it, after a year, only 74 had completed the new learning module on ME/CFS guidance. Meanwhile, as recently as last summer, the Department for Work and Pensions was still teaching its trainees elements of the old, discredited view of the condition. And, as the Liberal Democrat MP Tessa Munt, a hero of this story, tells me: “The piecemeal offerings in the government’s final delivery plan are not going to touch the system-wide failings.”

It’s not only the UK. I’ve been contacted by patients from around the world. In Sweden and Australia , official guidance still recommends GET and CBT. In Switzerland, I’m told, treatment is spiralling backwards, with a new wave of psychologisation. Norway, Finland and the Netherlands, despite their progressive medical reputations, sound like a waking nightmare for ME/CFS patients.

Of course, as there is no effective treatment, it’s a difficult situation for doctors as well as patients. But even worse than no solutions is false solutions, and a dangerous, gaslighting, even punitive approach to a terrible disease.

Across the decades, millions of people have been neglected, dismissed and mistreated, and still it goes on. We need to ask why so many patients have been abandoned, why discredited and dangerous treatments continue to be prescribed and why ignorance and neglect still dominate, in the health system and beyond. In other words, there has seldom been a stronger case for a public inquiry.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: In its push to subordinate women, the American right is embracing raunch
editorials.passage:
U nder Kash Patel, the FBI will now hire you even if you have a history of hiring prostitutes, or of having sex with animals. The rightwing Maha influencer Alex Clark had a guest on to her talk show to discuss the idea that wives should provide sex for their husbands on demand. A new ad for a sports gambling website is being hailed as a victory for the political right, because it features a nude Sydney Sweeney clutching footballs to her breasts. The Tate brothers , who encourage their male followers to pursue compulsive sexual conquest and who have been accused of sex trafficking and violence in the operation of their online cam porn business, have reportedly been friendly with members of Trump’s circle. A dizzying array of elites on both sides of the aisle – conservatives very much included – seem to have been socializing with a pedophile financier , and were so unfazed by his constant coterie of underaged girl companions that one begins to wonder whether they were habituated to such scenes. A prominent conservative writer , best known for her opposition to gender transition care for children, has announced a new book claiming to tackle the problem of young women who are supposedly unwilling to have enough sex. And the women of the president’s members club, Mar-A-Lago, are so well known for their dramatic facelifts, and their lips so stuffed with filler that they cannot quite close their mouths, that their faces are now a shorthand in the world of plastic surgery.

Raunch, vulgarity, a boorish entitlement to women’s sexual service, and the aesthetics – and, indeed, the business – of pornography are being embraced by the right.

For those old enough to remember the rise of Pat Buchanan and Phyllis Schlafly in the Reagan era, or even the earnest displays of Christian faith that characterized the George W Bush administration, this can all be a bit dizzying. For decades, it was the left that embraced public sexuality, taking the lead on comprehensive sex education, gay rights, and abortion access, and celebrating the sexual revolution that was ushered in by the advent of the birth control pill in the 1960s. It was liberals who embraced feminism, and worked to make women’s new freedom to delay marriage and childbearing enforcible in civil rights law. It was the left that retheorized family and marriage, reshaping the age-old institutions into ones that could better accommodate gay relationships and women’s equality. It was the progressives who embraced abortion as a means of sexual freedom and women’s self-determination, and who fought for birth control and sexually transmitted disease testing to be funded by the federal government. And it was the left that championed pornography as a free speech issue – shouting down the feminists in their own camp who critiqued the misogyny of its content, and making porn production and distribution into cornerstones of the liberal vision of the first amendment.

The right, meanwhile, was long married – pun intended – to a politics of sexual prohibition. When the Christian right was at the peak of its power, the Republican party had many of the same policies it does now: demanding bans on abortion, opposing gay rights, looking askance at birth control, pushing cuts to sexual health programs, rolling their eyes at civil rights protections meant to protect women workers from sexual harassment, and opposing comprehensive sex education, favoring instead abstinence-only models. But back then, when Evangelicism and the prim repression of the Protestant right were the dominant cultural force within the Republican party, these policies came packaged in a distinct style: one of sexual prohibition and shaming, that emphasized a kind of sexual self-discipline in the guise of decency. Back then, it really was a scandal when a pastor was caught cheating on his wife, even when his partner in infidelity was an adult woman. Sexual morality was a virtue that the right trumpeted in a very particular style: no sex until marriage, and even then, only the baby-making, heterosexual kind.

Was this all a ruse? The sexual morals of the Christian right seem to have evaporated as soon as the nation heard Donald Trump utter the words “grab ‘em by the pussy.” Now, an ostentatious lasciviousness reigns. In today’s Republican party, raunch is the coin of the realm, a “locker room talk” style of sexual vulgarity is de rigeur, and positions of power in the Trump world sometimes seem to go hand in hand with sexual assault allegations for men, and very specific kinds of surgical enhancements for women. The preachers have retreated, and the perverts have taken over. In the Maga era, sexual domination is synonymous with manliness, and porn is the lingua franca.

But is this really such a great change? After all, the transformation of the Republican party from a Christian culture that prioritized sexual prohibition to a pornified culture that celebrates sexual force has been a stylistic change, not a policy change: Republican politicians are still voting to make casual, premarital, non-procreative sex as dangerous, expensive, and risky as they can possibly make it – at least for women. If the left’s celebration of porn as a free speech issue always somewhat undermined their supposed commitment to women’s equality, the right’s onetime finger-wagging at pornography’s glorification of women’s sexual humiliation always clashed with the reality that the Christian right shared the same message and goal. Sexual prohibition and sexual force, after all, are just two different styles of what is ultimately a single project: the use of sex to subordinate women. At least now we can stop pretending that they’re not the same thing.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

editorials.title: The Coalition says it wants cheaper power, not ideology. But its evidence-free plan is all ideology
editorials.passage:
G ive the Coalition points for chutzpah, if nothing else. In a press release on Wednesday, first given to the Australian for a not exactly hard-won “exclusive”, it declared “Australians need cheaper power, not more ideology”.

You don’t have to get far beyond that headline to find its position comes from a worldview that is ideology on steroids. That worldview says climate breakdown is not real, or at least not a real concern, and Australia should abolish nearly all plans to respond to or prepare the economy – and people’s lives – for the changes under way.

As one campaigner put it, it is a plan to let climate change rip. Greenhouse gas emissions would be much higher than on the current trajectory.

From a here-and-now consumer point of view, it is a plan that is based on the fallacy that the big jump in power bills in recent years is due to renewable energy and a legislated net zero emissions target. Evidence and most experts clearly say otherwise. But both are disregarded.

Most of what the Coalition announced wasn’t actually new. The fresh bit is that it has promised to package up eight commitments in a new bill that would be introduced within 30 days if it was elected. Remarkably, at least half of those commitments are to abolish policies that were introduced under Coalition governments led by Scott Morrison, Tony Abbott and John Howard.

Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan say they would tear up the safeguard mechanism, introduced under Abbott, ostensibly to put a limit on pollution from major industrial sites. They would abolish the mid-century net zero emissions goal brought in by Morrison and Barnaby Joyce and legislated under Labor. They would repeal the Howard-era ban on nuclear energy.

They say they would scrap Labor’s capacity investment scheme, which is meant to underwrite solar, wind and energy storage developments, and replace it with a scheme that could also use public money to encourage fossil fuels and nuclear generation.

And they would abolish the vehicle efficiency standard that requires auto companies to lower the average emissions of their new car fleets – a policy that has belatedly seen a substantial increase in electric vehicle models available, including at the more affordable end, ending the farce in which Australians had far less opportunity to buy clean cars than any similar country.

Bizarrely, the Coalition claims the latter policy has somehow reduced vehicle choice. Tell that to the 25% of new car buyers who chose an EV last month – a higher percentage than bought a petrol or diesel car – and who are now enjoying much lower running costs.

Many of these policies are transparently Trumpian. They otherwise mostly fly in the face of global trends.

For the first time, renewable energy – solar, wind and hydro – last year overtook coal-fired power as the leading source of electricity. Solar energy capacity expanded by 30% in one year. According to the International Renewable Energy Agency, 85% of new power capacity built last year was renewable, and 90% of the renewables built were cheaper than the lowest fossil fuel alternative. Global EV sales are up more than 10% this year and expected to account for nearly 30% of the global total, with China leading the way .

Clean solutions are rising due to governments taking some action to reduce emissions and limit an accelerating climate crisis that is killing thousands of people . But cost is at least as big a factor, particularly in electricity generation.

In Australia, that argument has been muddied by events. As we have pointed out before , power bills increased dramatically after Russia’s attack on Ukraine sent global gas prices skyrocketing four years ago.

About the same time, coal power prices were pushed up by flooding at east coast mines and outages at ageing generators. Combined, these issues pushed up the wholesale cost of electricity by about 20% not long after Labor had overconfidently suggested that bills would come down by $275.

Despite claims to the contrary, renewable energy was not a major issue. Correlation is not causation. In fact, wholesale prices have fallen in some cases due to the influx of batteries that have allowed cheap excess solar power to be stored and used at night.

That’s the good news. The more complicated news is that replacing an old coal-fired system is expensive, however you do it. A renewables-dominated power system may not bring prices down much, if at all. But there is clear evidence that it will be cheaper than other options.

It will also cut heat-trapping pollution that is doing escalating damage and could allow an industrial shift that sets up Australians for a potential economic future as demand for fossil fuels falls.

This is not to say the Albanese government is doing enough. The renewables transition is at risk of slowing and new coal and gas export developments are still being approved . The prime minister gave a keynote speech at climate week in New York in which he avoided saying fossil fuels are the problem .

But Taylor goes further. On Wednesday, he implicitly dismissed climate change as a threat. He suggested all types of energy, dirty and clean, should be equally available. He claimed this would lower bills.

Evidence? That’s not how this ideology works.

Adam Morton is Guardian Australia’s climate and environment editor

editorials.title: OpenAI’s Medicare hack is a bleak opportunity for Australia to address its security shortcomings post-haste
editorials.passage:
Whoopsie! Dr Sam Altman Frankenstein regrets to inform you he’s lost control of his OpenAI monster.

It’s roving around doing things that provoke international legal investigation , and Australia has found out in the worst possible way.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, was obliged to announce from the United Nations summit on Thursday morning Australian time that an agentic AI from the OpenAI stable had gained unauthorised access to both public and non-public information from Australia’s Medicare website.

The good news in this debacle is that so far it appears no personal information held in Medicare’s records was compromised. Pursuing “a benign task” of compiling some health statistics, the portal breach accessed non-sensitive data about spending.

The good news, alas, ends here. OpenAI – a company worth US$852bn as per its last valuation – informed the government of the breach by … sending an email to its public email account three months after the hack occurred. Albanese revealed the date of Services Australia’s worst ever Inbox Zero was 10 September, and the Australian Cyber Security Centre was informed on 15 September.

Albanese at the UN has proved a fairly nimble diplomat, much to the surprise of anyone who has been on the receiving end of his vengeance at home. One imagines that a desire to soften fierce Trumpian pushback to Labor’s attempts at “digital duty-of-care” regulations for – ha! – AI and social media inspired the PM’s epically cringeworthy grip-and-grin selfie with the unpopular president. It was “photo diplomacy” wisely followed by a well-publicised hug with Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

After a direct meeting with Altman, the PM described the “obviously unacceptable” incident and his government’s “extreme concern”. Announcing immediate taskforces and urgent reviews into the breach and its national security implications, Albanese said Altman was aware “ the company had not done good enough ”.

“Aware” may actually be underselling it, because Altman has been making speeches of his own at the UN – to no less than the UN security council , alongside his supposed corporate rival, Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei – urging the governments of the world to collectively enforce regulations of the technology guided by democratic institutions.

Begging the question: Dr Frankenstein, what the hell’s been going on in your lab?

One longs for the tender innocence of last week when we could describe warnings from ex-Anthropic employees that AI could destroy the world within 10 years as merely utterly terrifying – because the attitude of the security council member representing the world’s richest democracy is that the “only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”.

Here’s hoping one will turn up. In the unregulated, commercial AI environment where “crawler” AIs are autonomously finding their way around sovereign data protection systems to scrape information, the explanatory metaphor that leaps to mind is if nuclear weapons had been retailed and the world only found out about radioactive fallout once a 10-year-old playing with it in a back yard had permanently depopulated Baltimore.

Is American laissez-faire fuckwittery to blame here? Yes – and Australians are right to be screaming that if OpenAI were a Chinese or Iranian company hacking into our systems ambassadors would be marching out of embassies with grand announcements and thundering speeches of condemnation.

But they’d also be wise to remember that geographically isolated, distant middle power Australia has only been afforded grandiosity on the world stage because in the post-second world war, pre-Trump era, it had the umbrella protection of a meaningful alliance with Daddy America.

And these days it’s Daddy America who’s a rules-free maniac whose sole political calculation is that money equals power and a literal “ to the victor the spoils ” foreign policy. To imagine Donald Trump’s US state department will be inspired into acts of responsibility due to Australian shaming it for data theft is some high genre alternate history. The man Trump pardoned who ran a stolen-data criminal marketplace spoke at the Republican convention in Dallas this year. Symbolic, no?

Internationally, the realignment of powers in the wake of Trump’s thuggery advances, but what role Australia will be offered in that realignment is uncertain, and it is narcissistic to pretend otherwise.

Locally, we’re not powerless. The Medicare breach is a bleak opportunity to address our revealed information security shortcomings post-haste, with full democratic transparency and accountability. All Australians should demand independent means to protect ourselves from the new front in the information war. If Albanese’s new taskforce determines that ministerial oversight failed to protect Medicare or any other comprised dataset, heads must – publicly – roll.

The ACTU has long been warning of US abrogation of AI security obligations, demanding the development of “sovereign AI” capacity to meet oncoming threats. Every one of us should back calls to regulate the living bejeezus out of all AI-capable foreign platforms seeking to operate here – or impose moratoriums on operations outright.

I am not entrusted to represent Australia diplomatically, so let me say to Mr Altman what a prime minister on a diplomatic mission apparently can’t: if your creatures are thieving our data and you are too much of a coward to pick up the damn phone to tell us, your destruction may be individual, it may be collective – but it is ensured. Van Badham is a Guardian Australia columnist

editorials.title: We’re in a crisis of loneliness – but is buying friends on an app likely to help solve it?
editorials.passage:
W hat price would you put on friendship? In these hyper-capitalistic times, where nothing is beyond being given a monetary value, perhaps even Mastercard wouldn’t dare to claim that it’s priceless. A YouGov survey found that 15% of Britons say they have no close friends, while nearly one in 10 (8%) have no friends at all. The numbers are similarly dismal in the US. As we face this contemporary crisis of connection, it is little wonder that friendship, or at least the possibility of it, is increasingly being marketed for sale.

There has been a striking increase in online platforms and apps that promise to introduce you – algorithmically, through social mixers or a combination – to your next BFF. There’s Cliq , PLY , standing for “People Like You”, and RealRoots which promises user satisfaction with the tagline: “Make new friends. Guaranteed”. Meanwhile, 222 boldly declares it is “not a friend-making service”, but a means to “explore serendipity” through social experiences with compatible people.

And this new sweep of pay-to-play friendships doesn’t stop at apps and algorithmic matchmaking. It is accompanied by supper clubs, book clubs, running clubs and other opportunities for you to mingle with people in your area – for a fee, of course. CircleUp , for example, holds regular social mixers across the UK for paying members, so that you can “keep seeing the same faces”. Others cultivate a more exclusive crowd. Gathering Tables hosts dinners for a “curated mix of guests”, united by their willingness to pay £145 a head.

These initiatives dangle community, but whether this trumps their commercial reason for being is debatable. The price of these apps and events is sometimes framed as a means of securing commitment, not just covering costs. “When you do things for free, people often don’t turn up,” PLY’s founder told the Guardian . But the effort becomes less civic-minded when you consider the desire for friendship is what makes these services valuable in the first place. These friend-making apps and paid-for gatherings may well offer opportunities for social connection – they are at least a date in the diary. But make no mistake, they exist primarily to encourage investment in a brand and even create opportunities to spend. Of course it is possible to make genuine connections in commercial spaces – many of us have made close bonds at work – but paying for introductions feels antithetical to the spirit of true friendship.

This new commercial interest in facilitating “gathering” speaks to the sense of collective untethering from community. Many of us understand we are lacking community, perhaps even more than friendship. It is unsettlingly common to hear people complaining of their current social network, as though a more suitable or nourishing one already exists, just waiting for you to slot into it. No wonder brands are attempting to package them up.

Cliq claims the first step to “start your community” is to download its app. But real community is built, not bought (and certainly not downloaded). It takes time, shared investment and often some weathering on both sides . It is certainly possible that meaningful, enduring ties can begin at a paid-for meet-up. But while the payment can create the conditions for friendship, it can’t manufacture the friendship itself.

Tellingly, ease is often central to the offering: Cliq claims “finding your people shouldn’t be difficult”. Shouldn’t it? No matter how you meet, it takes time and effort to turn an acquaintance into a friend; that same process, multiplied and sustained, is what creates a community. Seeking shortcuts or higher-quality connections is not only beside the point, it works against the rewards: authentic relationships can only be forged without expectation of a return on investment.

That’s not to say we don’t need more places and opportunities to meet new people; the very existence of these services at least demonstrates that we do. But before entrusting our need for greater intimacy and affection to a third party, we might ask ourselves if we could be doing more to put ourselves out there socially. Could we extend an invitation to friendly strangers, or introduce our mutuals and turn acquaintances into friends?

The best community-building exercise I’ve heard of lately was before a performance of Austentatious – the Jane Austen comedy play – where all solo ticket-holders were invited to come early and mingle before the show. The event was free, organised around a preexisting commitment and people could opt in. There was the opportunity to meet people; the work, and potential reward, of making a new friend was left to you.

Elle Hunt is a freelance journalist
