editorials.title: Britain would not cut up the Bayeux tapestry. So seize this moment and reunite the Parthenon sculptures in Greece
editorials.passage:
F or the first time in nearly 1,000 years, the Bayeux tapestry is back in Britain . Its arrival is a significant cultural moment, and a reminder that, in an age of social media and ubiquitous screens, historic objects still capture the public imagination.

The British Museum describes the tapestry as one of the “wonders of the medieval world”. But the museum already houses many wonders, including one that is instantly recognisable: the Parthenon sculptures, chiselled away and illegally removed from Athens to be taken to Britain more than two centuries ago by Lord Elgin.

There are striking similarities between the two pieces. Both were conceived as single works, intended to be seen and understood as a whole. In the case of the Parthenon sculptures, that relationship is also architectural: they were created as inseparable elements of the monument itself. Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it. Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures. A single masterpiece was divided, and its surviving parts are now principally split between London and Athens.

The sculptures tell a story of unique historical importance. Not only of gods and heroes, but also of ordinary civil life in ancient Athens. They gave a visual expression in stone to the religious, civic and political identity of fifth-century Athens. The Parthenon frieze, in particular, remains one of the world’s most compelling representations of the collective life of the city from which democracy emerged. It is a powerful celebration of Athenian democracy.

Unlike the sculptures, the Bayeux tapestry survives as one continuous work, measuring nearly 70 metres. It too tells a story, from the events preceding the Norman Conquest to the battle of Hastings and the death of Harold. Its wonder lies not just in the individual scenes, but in the way they are experienced together as a whole.

The case for reunification is not an argument for emptying the world’s museums. The Parthenon constitutes a specific and exceptional case. The issue is not merely one of possession or legal title. It concerns the restoration of the physical, aesthetic and conceptual integrity of a dismembered monument of outstanding universal value.

The surviving sculptures should be viewed together, at the same time, within sight of the monument for which they were created. The Acropolis Museum was designed specifically to make this possible.

Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum’s ownership of the sculptures , or a scheme that would mean we “borrow” parts of our own monument. And the British public is increasingly on Greece’s side. A nationally representative poll published last year found that a majority supports the return of the sculptures to Greece. More strikingly, 72% agreed that they are best understood as part of a single ensemble with the Parthenon.

For decades, Greece has been in dialogue with Britain to achieve that goal. In recent years, my government has held detailed discussions with the leadership of the British Museum about how reunification might be achieved. I was, therefore, surprised at the recent suggestion from the Museum that the Bayeux tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures. I do not believe it does.

France has lent the artwork as an undivided whole, and that work will return to France as an undivided whole. The Parthenon presents the reverse situation: integral parts of the monument were forcibly removed and dispersed. Our objective is their permanent reunification. Unesco’s Intergovernmental Committee for the Return of Cultural Property to Countries of Origin has repeatedly called upon the UK to engage with Greece on this matter in good-faith dialogue .

Reunification could become the foundation of a broad and enduring cultural partnership between our countries, creating new opportunities for exhibitions, scholarship, conservation and exchanges between Greek and British museums. Together we could create a new model of cultural cooperation between two democratic nations and allies with deeply shared values and ideals. That is the prize.

In 2023, before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham urged that the sculptures be sent back “ no strings attached ”, adding: “Let’s use culture to change how Britain is seen around the world.” I could not agree more.

At a time when democratic principles are being challenged all over the world, restoring the unity of a monument so closely associated with the emergence of democracy itself would send a powerful signal. Greece remains ready. What is needed now is the political will and courage to take the decisive step, to reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship.

Kyriakos Mitsotakis is the prime minister of Greece

editorials.title: Liberia is squandering the moral authority it claims at the UN
editorials.passage:
For the past nine months, Liberia has used its experiences of prolonged armed conflict to serve as a principled voice in United Nations debates about the humanitarian consequences of a number of the most intractable geopolitical crises – from Gaza and Sudan to Ukraine and Iran.

Yet, hidden beneath this virtuous veneer lies a troubling contradiction. As my country prepares to assume the rotating presidency of the UN Security Council (UNSC) in December as a non-permanent member, it is flouting our Constitution and contravening UN conventions by hosting deportees expelled from the United States.

A year before its current charm offensive across the Atlantic – where a delegation led by the president is now courting American lawmakers in Washington and broadcasting its peace and security agenda at UN General Assembly convenings in New York – Liberia signed an agreement on September 10, 2025 with the Trump administration to accommodate an undisclosed number of third-country nationals deported from the US.

Since January 2025, the Trump administration has struck deportation agreements with 35 countries, almost a third of them in Africa, to receive foreigners whose US immigration statuses range from regularised (and legal) to protected from removal. Liberia’s cooperation is one of the largest and has proved particularly controversial.

Late last month, the first 20 of an expected 1,200 deportees arrived in a widely reported – and condemned – handover at Roberts International Airport (RIA). In a dramatic turn of events, the six who refused to disembark were whisked off to Equatorial Guinea under opaque terms. For those still in Liberia, it is equally unclear who they are, why they were deported, where they will reside, whether they are free to leave, and what legal standing they possess.

Although the agreement between Monrovia and Washington is skimpy on the details, it remains politically fraught, ethically suspect and illegal. Deportations without due process, and involving cruel and inhumane treatment, contravene principles within the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Consenting to host third-country nationals without legislative approval breaches Article 34(f) of Liberia’s Constitution.

Several deportees who landed at RIA on August 20 said they had been detained in the US without due process, contrary to articles 8 and 10 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which guarantee the right to an “effective remedy” and a “fair and public hearing” before an independent court or tribunal. They also said they had been chained during the flight to Liberia, treatment that may violate Article 5, which states that “no one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment”.

Other UN agreements which may have been flouted include the 1967 Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees, the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to which both Liberia and the US are parties.

On the home front, Liberia’s Constitution states plainly that any “treaties, conventions and such other international agreements negotiated or signed on behalf of the Republic” must be ratified by the National Legislature. Our Legislature neither deliberated on nor approved the agreement to host third-country nationals, which was unilaterally authorised by the executive. On that basis, implementing the agreement without legislative approval is unconstitutional.

By accepting mostly Black and brown deportees under such questionable arrangements, Liberia is complicit in executing “make America white again”-era expulsions that would shame its founding mothers and fathers who fled 19th-century chattel slavery and racial discrimination in the US. This small West African country – once a 21st-century poster child for post-war stability – has undercut any credibility it might wield in UNSC deliberations going forward. So, what exactly do Liberian policymakers in the executive branch of government hope to gain?

As a scholar who researches migration to/from/within Liberia, I was naturally curious about the terms, conditions and implications of Liberia’s bilateral agreement with the US. An official press release issued two days before the first batch of deportees was expected turned my curiosity into suspicion. It spins the agreement as a “humanitarian” arrangement for the “dignified, safe and orderly transfer” of non-criminals removed from the US. It also claims that although Liberia had “not demanded or received any compensation or promise of reward”, “support” would be available for managing the programme and strengthening migration management.

The word “support” deliberately muddles the truth. Why would a low-income country agree to host up to 1,200 third-country nationals without monetary incentives when the Trump administration previously paid five foreign governments more than $32m collectively to accept roughly 300 deportees? Nothing added up, so I went looking for answers.

I encountered evasion at every turn. The minister of foreign affairs said she could not share the agreement with me because it was “at the level of the National Security Council”. Instead, she forwarded me the press release I had already read – and doubted – as a consolation. The president’s national security adviser feigned ignorance. The National Security Agency director admitted he had the agreement and would get back to me. I am still awaiting his response. And Liberia’s then minister of justice, who has since assumed the role of acting minister of defence, declared haughtily that the agreement remained classified because it was entered into with a “foreign country”.

Despite these policymakers’ lack of transparency, I discovered the agreement hidden in plain sight on the US State Department website. It raised alarm not only because of what it says, but also because of what it leaves out, particularly the legitimacy of expelling third-country nationals whose protection claims in the US are pending, as well as rewarding a foreign government [Liberia] for facilitating this. If The New York Times’ August 21 story is anything to go by, Trump administration officials agreed to pay Liberia $5m for accepting deportees. Not only does this contradict claims of receiving no “compensation or promise of reward”, but remuneration also violates Article 34(f) of Liberia’s Constitution because it was not approved by the National Legislature.

Other questions loom. How was the $5m negotiated and by whom? What exactly does funding cover? How are resources being channelled if not through Liberia’s budget? Who manages the money? How are expenses monitored and reported? These questions are particularly salient because, if New York Times compensation figures are accurate, the amount allocated for Liberia is significantly less than what other governments have collected for accepting fewer deportees. Rwanda, for example, received $7.5m to accept just seven people.

My country has a long track record of signing dubious deals with the US. Most recently, the US-Liberia Bilateral Health Cooperation Memorandum of Understanding was signed last December. In exchange for more than $124m in planned “assistance” from the Trump administration, Liberia handed over access to its citizens’ health data without our permission. Similar aid pacts have been rejected or resisted by several other African governments. Although Liberia’s government has never publicly released the memorandum of understanding, one could argue that it too violates Article 34(f) of the Constitution since legislative approval was not granted.

Exactly a century ago – in 1926 – Liberia finalised another agreement with the US that undermined its sovereignty. Heavily indebted and desperate to ward off French and British colonisers, it accepted under duress a $5m loan from the Finance Corporation of America, a private subsidiary of US-based Firestone Tyre and Rubber Company. This was in exchange for signing a 99-year lease of 404,700 hectares (one million acres), enabling Firestone to extract unprocessed rubber at a measly six cents per acre. Loan terms authorised the US president to appoint Americans as administrators of Liberia’s finances, and forbade Liberia from borrowing without Firestone’s written consent. This set into motion an enduring legacy of US resource extraction from which Liberia has never recovered.

If Liberia is to assume its rightful place as Africa’s first independent Black republic – and a post-war “success story” at that – it must cancel bilateral agreements with the US that weaken its autonomy, violate national laws and erode citizens’ trust. It must actively pursue “positive peace”, the absence of structural violence, in the corridors of power both at home and abroad.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: To the victor belong Venezuela’s spoils: Delcy Rodriguez’s UNGA about-face
editorials.passage:
Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez took to the stage yesterday at the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York City to deliver a rather bland speech, in which she thanked United States President Donald Trump for resuming “diplomatic relations and cooperation” with Venezuela.

This was a different vibe, to be sure, than the one she opted for at the same venue in September 2019, when, as vice president under Nicolas Maduro, she accused the US of perpetrating “economic terrorism” that did not require the use of bombs “but rather through banks and insurance companies”.

Denouncing the global superpower’s militarisation of international relations and punishment of millions of innocent people “in order to apply regime change doctrines and steal other nations’ resources”, the Rodriguez of 2019 went on to cite Venezuelan economic losses to the tune of $130bn between 2015 and 2018 alone on account of US sanctions.

She additionally offered her opinion that the domination of the US political system by “plutocratic minorities” made the country unqualified to impose its model on other countries.

Seven years later, US plutocracy is going strong with Trump at the helm – the same Trump alongside whom a grinning Rodriguez appeared in a photograph taken in New York on Tuesday, less than nine months after he oversaw regime change in Venezuela by kidnapping Maduro .

The kidnapped president is now also in New York, albeit in jail, and is scheduled to stand trial in June 2027 . This despite his attempts to remind everyone that, as a sitting head of state, his prosecution in a foreign court contravenes international law.

Then again, abducting other countries’ presidents is also pretty glaringly illegal. But Trump has made it clear that he alone is in charge of deciding what is and is not permissible on any given day.

The abduction took place on January 3, when the US military launched air attacks on Venezuela, killing some 100 people and whisking Maduro and his wife away.

He is accused of an array of misdeeds, including being the leader of the “Cartel of the Suns” – which, mind you, does not actually exist – and engaging in “conspiracy to possess machineguns and destructive devices”.

This is quite the accusation coming from the country that just used all manner of destructive devices to bomb Venezuela and kill a bunch of people.

Anyway, bald-faced hypocrisy is nothing new in the land of the “plutocratic minorities”.

Now, the waning corporate media interest in Maduro’s fate amounts to another coup for US impunity, as folks go about more or less forgetting that there is a foreign head of state sitting in a Brooklyn prison.

But Maduro’s disappearance works out well for Rodriguez, as she goes about enabling the very theft of resources she once decried.

Rodriguez took the stage at the UN the day after Trump, who used the platform to pat himself on the back for the trampling of Venezuelan sovereignty that conveniently culminated in last month’s announcement from the White House of the “biggest oil deal in world history”, securing US majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves.

Speaking to his international audience, Trump boasted: “To the victor belong the spoils. You’ve all heard that.”

Never mind that you’re not technically supposed to admit that you attacked a country just to get its oil. (You’re also not, in polite company, supposed to threaten to annihilate Iran – another of Trump’s UN talking points.)

Since January, the US has lifted many coercive economic measures against Venezuela (including against Rodriguez herself), easing the brutal sanctions regime that as of 2020 was estimated to have already killed 100,000 Venezuelans, according to former UN independent expert Alfred-Maurice de Zayas.

But trading sanctions for de facto colonialism isn’t a great deal, either.

Meanwhile, Trump’s continued manic bombing of vessels in the Caribbean and Pacific, which a recent UN report warned may constitute crimes against humanity, suggests the US is nowhere near to kicking its old habit of terrorism – and is all the more reason that Rodriguez might have refrained from thanking the US leader for his “cooperation”.

As Gregory Wilpert, founder of the Venezuelanalysis website and author of Changing Venezuela by Taking Power, diplomatically put it to me: “One cannot help but wonder whether Delcy Rodriguez is over-complying with Trump in some aspects of her negotiations with him.”

Noting that Rodriguez is “in a highly vulnerable position”, Wilpert ran through a few of the options she faces, such as “the possibility that the Trump administration could treat her as it treated Maduro – by attempting to kidnap her – or as it treated Iran, by targeting the country’s highest levels of government”.

Or, Wilpert said, there is always the Cuba approach, which would entail “the kind of economic siege” that is undertaken “with the aim of starving an entire country”.

In her UN address, Rodriguez promised that Venezuela would hold elections at some unspecified point in time – not that the US, for its part, really cares about democracy as long as the right people are in power.

And although it’s still too early to tell, Rodriguez might just be one of those people.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: Before election commissioners flagged ‘centralisation’ of voter rolls, it was done in Bengal SIR
editorials.passage:
Vivek Joshi, one of India’s three election commissioners, raised an internal alarm in May about the “gradual centralisation” of voter lists, The Indian Express reported in its investigation about divisions within the top leadership of the Election Commission on Wednesday.

By then, however, the process of drawing up the electoral roll of West Bengal had already been centralised despite fervent opposition. In fact, the issue of centralisation came up repeatedly in political debates and courtroom hearings during the six-month-long special intensive revision of voter lists in the state.

Eventually, the names of over 91 lakh voters were deleted from Bengal’s rolls even though almost a third of them submitted documents and attended hearings to challenge their exclusion. The scale of deletions proved to be significant in shaping the results of the Assembly elections that took place in April, as Scroll has previously reported.

Neither the Election Commission nor the Supreme Court followed the principle of decentralisation, which is clearly established in the law that governs the drawing up of electoral rolls in India.

Section 13B of The Representation of the People Act of 1950 states that voter lists for every Assembly constituency “shall be prepared and revised by an electoral registration officer”. These officers are supposed to be local government officials who are appointed by the Election Commission “in consultation” with state governments to fulfil this responsibility.

But in Bengal, their power was systematically curtailed by an overbearing Election Commission, while the Supreme Court dithered in deciding on the legal validity of its actions. Here is a recap of how this was done:

The special intensive revision of voter lists turned controversial in Bengal after the Election Commission began issuing notices to some of those 7.1 crore voters who had submitted the enumeration forms that it had earlier asked them to fill out.

Notices were sent to voters who were unable to show that either they or their parents were voters in 2002. In addition to this, a whopping 1.4 crore voters received notices for what the Election Commission called “logical discrepancies”.

These were voters whose forms were flagged for name or gender mismatch with their entries in the 2002 voter list. Several voters were summoned for hearings because the number of siblings they had or their age gap with their parents or grandparents was deemed unusual.

The notices were generated centrally using software which flagged issues in the forms that voters had submitted. It is unclear how the Election Commission came up with the criteria that were laid down for flagging voters.

Section 22 of The Representation of the People Act of 1950 only empowers a local bureaucrat called the electoral registration officer to correct and delete entries from the voter rolls. They can do so on their own or if they receive an application for doing so, provided they are “satisfied” after conducting an inquiry that the entry in question is erroneous.

But on the ground in Bengal, electoral registration officers complained that they had no say in generating these notices. “We have no power to decide which elector will be called for a hearing,” one such officer from Nadia district told The Indian Express in December, adding that the notices were “automatically generated”.

An association of state government employees even wrote to the Election Commission outlining their concerns about the process.

“Names of electors might be deleted from the electoral roll without the knowledge of the ERO [electoral registration officer],” wrote Saikat Asraf Ali, general secretary of the West Bengal Civil Service (Executive) Officers’ Association. “The common people who will be affected by such action will only blame the ERO without knowing that the ERO has been kept out of the entire deletion process by the commission.”

Those who received these notices had to then show up for hearings. The law states that the “electoral registration officer shall give the person concerned a reasonable opportunity of being heard” before taking any action. While it allows these officers to employ other persons to assist them in the task of drawing up the rolls, the final decision with regard to inclusion or deletion of voters must be theirs.

However, this provision was turned on its head in Bengal. The Reporters’ Collective reported at the time that the Election Commission inserted observers into the exercise and gave them a veto over decisions made by the electoral registration officers.

Petitioners who had challenged the constitutional validity of the revision process in Bengal before the Supreme Court also took up this issue . The Election Commission asserted in court that the power of the observers was “limited to assisting the EROs [electoral registration officers] in the decision-making process”.

On February 9, the court accepted this assertion at face value and reiterated that “the final decision will be taken by the EROs [electoral registration officers] only”. Despite this, the cases of more than 60 lakh voters who attended hearings and produced documents remained undecided with Assembly elections just around the corner.

Taking note of the “extraordinary” situation, the Supreme Court decided to transfer these cases to judicial officers. That is how The Representation of the People Act of 1950, which vests the power to determine the eligibility of voters only in the office of the electoral registration officer, was cast aside.

The judicial officers restored the names of about 33 lakh voters to the electoral roll ahead of the election. But more than 27 lakh voters were deprived of their right to vote.

The Indian Express investigation published on Wednesday does not mention these 27 lakh voters. It instead cites the example of Goa, where electoral registration officers repeatedly complained in February that the Election Commission’s software did not let them include the names of 97 voters with “logical discrepancies” whom they had found to be genuine.

Electoral registration officers decide to include or exclude voters on the basis of the documents that are submitted before them. The special intensive revision of voter rolls in Bengal saw even this simple procedure becoming centralised and, therefore, controversial.

First, the Election Commission put out a list of documents which officers were supposed to accept. Its list did not include Aadhaar, the document with the maximum coverage across India. When the Supreme Court ordered that Aadhaar be added to the list, the poll body worked around this by asking officers to seek additional documents from voters it summoned for hearings.

The Election Commission also opposed proposals to consider Class X admit cards issued by the West Bengal Board of Secondary Education for voters who were sent notices. Notably, the letter turning down one such proposal came from the poll body’s head office in Delhi.

The decision affected voters in rural Bengal who have few other documents in their possession. Civil society organisations and political parties once again went to the Supreme Court to challenge it. Ultimately, this question was settled in favour of accepting Class X admit cards, but along with pass certificates.

Notwithstanding this particular decision, constitutional law experts have criticised the Supreme Court’s handling of the special intensive revision of voter rolls in Bengal. Lawyer Gautam Bhatia wrote an op-ed piece likening the approach adopted by the court to that of an “administrator”. The Supreme Court, he argued , had restricted its interventions to minutiae while allowing the process, on the whole, to continue.

“It is worth remembering that in a constitutional democracy, the Court’s primary role is to ensure that other state organs comply with the Constitution, and not to transform itself into an administrator,” Bhatia wrote in The Hindu .

The controversy over the role of the judiciary, in fact, predates the conduct of the roll revision exercise in Bengal. In December itself, The Indian Express had reported that notices were being generated centrally and not by electoral registration officers in Bihar, the first state where the special intensive revision of voter lists was carried out last year.

The issue came up before the Supreme Court when it was hearing a challenge pertaining to the process in Bihar. The petitioners argued that the Election Commission had ignored Rule 21A of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 . These rules lay down the process of verification to be followed by the electoral registration officer before deleting the names of voters.

In May 2026, the court upheld the new process, saying that the 1960 rules should not be read in an “unduly restrictive manner”. The new rules differed from the “form” of Rule 21A, but the “substance remains intact”, the two-judge bench led by the chief justice said in its judgement.

editorials.title: Delhi history: How Sanjay Gandhi’s ‘beautification’ drive cost the Congress its goodwill
editorials.passage:
Formed in 1955, the Delhi Development Authority’s remit was to create order out of urban chaos and build housing for the capital’s growing army of civil servants. Clusters of DDA flats, modelled on apartment complexes in the Soviet bloc, sprang up on vacant land. The DDA was also the sole developer of agricultural land needed for the city’s expansion, earning it huge profits. In one instance, four farming brothers were paid one rupee per square metre of land; the same land was later sold to a commercial developer for Rs 200,000 per square metre. After a 14-year court battle, the brothers were awarded compensation of 2 million rupees.

The mid-1970s would witness a convergence of two egos that exposed the huge gap between the wealthy and the powerful and those living on the margins of society. Indira’s son Sanjay, the leader of the Congress Party’s youth wing and, as Rana Dasgupta writes, “the first of Delhi’s [many] political bad boys”, had embraced the cause of the city’s beautification – in other words, the demolition of slums and the relocation of their residents to resettlement camps on the other side of the Yamuna River, where conditions were often inhumane. He found an ally in Jagmohan Malhotra, the DDA’s ambitious vice-chairman. Jagmohan’s idol was Baron Haussmann, whom he credited with transforming Paris, once “an ugly and despicable town”, into a “seat of vigorous and vibrant culture” by clearing slums and building grand boulevards.

Sanjay found the slums that had grown up around Turkman Gate in the Old City particularly irksome because they obscured the view of the Jama Masjid from Connaught Place. On April 19, 1976, bulldozers flanked by two platoons of police started demolishing a cluster of 50 hutments. Fearful that their homes might be next, residents appealed to Jagmohan, who is said to have replied: “Do you think we were mad to destroy one Pakistan to create another one?” When the demolitions resumed, a group of burqa-clad women and their children squatted on the road, defying the bulldozers to run over them. As they stood up to pray, police began throwing stones and using tear gas to disperse the protesters.

In the hours that followed, dozens of people were killed (some estimates put the figure at over a thousand; Jagmohan maintained that only six died). Residents fleeing into the Faize-Elahi Mosque, believing they would be safe, came under police attack. “In just half an hour the Masjid had become an abattoir. Blood lay in pools on the ground and the air was noxious with fumes of tear gas and groans and moans of the injured congregation,” survivors told the journalists, John Dayal and Ajoy Bose. After a curfew was declared at 5.30 pm, the bulldozers moved in again, while police broke into homes, looting their contents and raping women. What remained of the slum at Turkman Gate was scooped up into trucks and dumped behind Delhi’s Ring Road, where for days afterwards “buzzards and jackals were seen rummaging through the rubble”.

Adding to the trauma of Delhi’s slum dwellers was the targeting of males as part of Sanjay’s vasectomy drive. Across India, more than six million men were subjected to a campaign of forced sterilisation, 15 times the number sterilised by the Nazis. Officials who didn’t meet their quotas found themselves sacked from their jobs or evicted from their government housing, turning the campaign into a brutal and arbitrary process that disproportionately affected the poorest and most powerless. In the basement of Dujana House, the main sterilisation centre in Old Delhi, Dayal and Bose described how doctors and nurses conducted “rapid-fire operations on their screaming victims”.

In January 1977, Indira revoked the Emergency, believing her ruthless pattern of rule could continue under the cloak of democracy. The gamble backfired spectacularly. When the election results were announced, Congress had won just 154 seats, its worst performance to date. Her old foe Morarji Desai became prime minister and leader of the Janata Party alliance. India’s first experiment in coalition government soon degenerated into infighting. When fresh elections were called in 1980, Indira pulled off one of the most remarkable comebacks in Indian political history, securing an outright majority of 351 in the 524-seat Lok Sabha. With his mother back in office, Sanjay was made Congress general secretary, prompting spe­culation that he was being groomed to take over the prime ministership. But on June 23, 1980, shortly after taking off from Delhi’s Safdarjung Airport, his stunt plane crashed, killing him and his copilot instantly. Distraught and lonely, Indira turned to her eldest son, Rajiv, a commercial airline pilot with no experience or interest in politics, to fill the breach. In 1981, he was elected to the Lok Sabha from the family’s traditional constituency of Amethi in Uttar Pradesh.

Indira’s assassination unleashed the worst communal violence since Partition, as Hindus turned against Sikhs in cities across northern India. In New Delhi, police refused to intervene as mobs went house to house to exact vengeance. Estimates put the number of Sikhs killed in the capital at between 3,000 and 10,000. Homes and businesses were set alight, the arsonists armed with addresses of Sikh families handed out to them by members of Congress. “For many of my generation, who were children or teenagers in 1984, the Sikh riots were the foundational coming-of-age experience, revealing, as they seemed to do, the deep truth of Delhi’s social relations,” writes Dasgupta. “Bloodshed, it seemed, had not ended with Indian independence. This time it could not be blamed on the British, or on Pakistan, or on the insider within. It was eternally inherent to the city.” Rajiv Gandhi, who was sworn in as prime minister within hours of his mother’s death, shrugged off the massacres, callously remarking: “When a big tree falls, the earth shakes.” Despite ten government-appointed commissions, only 30 people, mostly low-ranking Congress supporters, were convicted for their role in the attacks.

The wave of sympathy unleashed by Indira’s assassination saw Congress win the December 1984 elections by a massive landslide. But Rajiv squandered his mandate. In the 1989 election, the party saw its majority more than halved, with the poor showing blamed on his lack of political experience and allegations of corruption and cronyism. When the fragile coalition that took power collapsed in March 1991, an early election was called, but Rajiv would not be around to contest it. On 21 May 1991, a suicide bomber sent by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam assassinated him as he was campaigning in Tamil Nadu. This time, the Indian capital remained peaceful.

Excerpted with permission from The Shortest History of Delhi, John Zubrzycki, Hachette India.

editorials.title: Yemen’s Houthi conflict has roots deeper than religion
editorials.passage:
The current Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen poses a serious challenge to the energy supply chain through the Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world's most critical maritime chokepoints. Following the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb has emerged as a new theatre of conflict between Saudi Arabia and Houthi forces. The conflict between the two is not new. It is deep and wide and is anchored in the ethno-religious rivalry. Yemen's ethno-religious and tribal landscapes are complex and fractured.

Geography, ancient tribal confederations, and Islamic legal schools determine the country's power dynamics. Around 65 per cent of Yemen's population follows Sunni Islam and is geographically distributed across the coastal plains, the eastern desert expanses, and the southern uplands. They follow the Islamic jurisprudence of the Shafi'i school. Nearly 35 per cent of Yemenis are Shia Muslims. They follow the Zaydi School of Islamic jurisprudence. This branch of Shia Islam is unique to Yemen. Zaydi demography is concentrated primarily in the rugged northern highlands, particularly in Sa'ada, Amran, and Sana'a. They have a rich political history spanning a millennium in northern Yemen.

The Houthi movement springs from the Zaydi revivalist identity. A small minority of Ismaili Shias live in the Haraz mountains. Non-Muslim demography is microscopic. The ancient Jewish people living in Yemen have emigrated to Israel, and maybe a handful of them live in the north. A very small number of Hindus and Christians live in Aden.

Tribal affiliation also determines social identity in Yemen. It is a powerful social force. Tribalism plays a vital role in governance, resource distribution, and conflict resolution. The tribal and ethnic consciousness among 70 to 80 per cent of the Yemenis is strong and inalterable. The Yemeni tribes are organised around four distinct historical and tribal confederations. They traditionally identify their roots in ancient kingdoms. The Hashid confederation is the most cohesive and politically organised one. It is located in the northern highlands, namely the Amran and Sana'a governorates.

The Confederacy has historically been led by the Al-Ahmar family. The Hashid is a more centralised confederation. Bakil, on the other hand, is the largest tribal confederation. It covers the vast swathes of the north and east of Sana'a. It comprises sub-tribes like the Khawlan and Dihm. The Houthi movement (Ansar Allah) draws significant tribal support from Bakil territory.

The Madhhaj Confederation is situated in central and southern Yemeni regions of Marib, Al-Bayda, and Shabwa. Madhhaj's shifting political realities have not dented its internal alliances. The Himyar confederation is located largely in the southern mountainous regions and coastal plains. Madhhaj and Himyar follow the Shafi'i school of Islamic jurisprudence. They are a cultural contrast to the Zaydi Shia tribal headquarters of the far north. However, Yemeni tribalism is not uniform. Their governance structures are also different. Northern Yemen is known for a rigid armed hierarchy. It is controlled by the Hashid and Bakil and mostly by the Zaydi Shia sect. They function as autonomous political and military groups.

Madhhaj and Himyar, by contrast, dominate Southern Yemen and adhere primarily to the Shafi'i school of jurisprudence. British colonial rule and socialist experiments in South Yemen have seemingly softened the traditional tribal structures. But they are acutely conscious of their regional or civic identities. The eastern hinterlands constitute the Mahra and Hadhramaut regions. They embody distinct cultural and tribal structures. The Mahra Sultanate’s legacy in the east continues to foster a strong ethno-linguistic bond, especially for the non-Arabic Mahri language.

The Mahri language plays a vital role in the intra-tribal unity in the east. In Hadhramaut, the Hadhramaut Tribal Alliance (HTA) is a powerful regional defence bloc. Tribal laws ('Urf) in the north are stronger. They decide matters such as security, conflict mediation, and resource distribution. They are a powerful parallel jurisprudence. The tribal jurisprudence in Yemen follows a structured hierarchy comprising tribal elders, Sheikhs, and the Maraga (the apex tribal authority and the final appellate body).

Given the above tribal antecedents and stakeholdership, the Houthis (known as Ansar Allah or "Supporters of God") emerged in the late 1990s as a Zaydi Shiite Muslim revivalist movement in the difficult and rugged Saada province of northern Yemen. The Zaydi Shiite Muslim revivalist movement emerged in the early 1990s. It was based on issues concerning the identity of northern Yemen’s Zaydi community, predominantly Shiite. Zaydis follow Shiite Islam, named after Zayd ibn Ali.

The Zaydi Imamate exercised its authority in northern Yemen for 1000 years until the republican revolution in 1962. The revolution brought to power a new government in Yemen that was antagonistic towards Zaydis. The Saudi funding of Salafi/Wahhabi ideology and centres in Zaydi territories intensified the matter. The locals assumed that the Saudi funding might lead to Sunni fundamentalism, indoctrination of Zaydi youth and cultural infiltration in northern Yemen.

In response to Saudi Salafism, Zaydi cultural revivalism assumed salience in 1992. It also gave rise to a network called Shabab al-Mu'minin, the Believing Youth. Its mission was to revive traditional Zaydi history, theology, tradition and jurisprudence as a counterweight to Saudi Salafism. The initiative witnessed resounding success. The revivalist tendency soon gave rise to a rebel group led by Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi.

The word 'Houthi' comes from his name. He was at the helm of efforts to radicalise the Zaydi youth in the north. He transformed the growing resentment and genuine grievances into a political doctrine and identity politics in the early 2000s. He projected the Zaydis' problems as both religious and political. He accused the central Yemeni government of corruption and subordination to Saudi Arabia and the US. He also indulged in political sloganeering, which bordered on hate speech. His death in a military clash in 2004 did not quell the movement. It made him a martyr and radically changed the Believing Youth's religious revival into an anti-government armed militia. It is known today as the Houthis.

The Houthis reincarnated as a dominant national force from a non-descript mountain militia. The political methodology that brought the Houthis to political prominence is resistance to Salafism in Zaydi heartlands; charged, violent anti-government, anti-imperialist, anti-Israel, and anti-Western sentiment; objection to northern Yemen’s economic marginalisation; the central government's corruption, institutional and infrastructural neglect, and antipathy; and clever and pragmatic political alliances.

The Houthis made the most out of the Arab Spring in 2011. The collapse of President Saleh and the emergence of a weak transitional government helped the Houthis to expand their territory and move beyond the northern mountains.

The tactical and pragmatic political alliances with some of their political adversaries, especially ex-President Saleh, helped the Houthis to seize Sanaa in September 2014 and to assess the military power of the central government. At this vantage point, the Houthis could project themselves as defenders of Yemen against what they portrayed as Saudi aggression, intervention and foreign invasion.

The Houthis' emergence as a strong regional force stems from their control of key stretches of the Red Sea coast. Their current military strength, continuous military support from Iran and seizure of territories make them increasingly lethal and a formidable force that currently holds the capacity to disrupt global shipping lanes, Saudi oil networks, and the global energy crisis, and launch long-range missile strikes.

(Jajati K Pattnaik is a Professor and Chairperson at the Centre for West Asian Studies, School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi. Chandan Panda is a Professor at the Central University of Karnataka, Karnataka. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the authors. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: A greeting on the tarmac breaking protocol and a verdict: Trump-Xi summit already has a clear winner
editorials.passage:
The video shared by Reuters on X of Donald Trump breaking protocol and welcoming Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews late Wednesday afternoon (US time) was revealing for more reasons than one. This was the first time in 11 years that a US president had taken the pains to be present at the airport to receive a foreign head of state. The last instance was Barack Obama receiving Pope Francis in 2015.

The special gesture extended to the rolling out of a 100-ft-long red carpet on the tarmac beside Xi’s plane at the Maryland military base, the playing of a military band, cannons blasting ceremonial fire and a B-1 military bomber flying overhead. Trump appeared on his best behaviour, trying to simultaneously appease and impress Xi. The Chinese side won’t be complaining.

As the aeroplane came to a halt and Chinese officials slowly descended the stairs one by one, Trump and Melania were seen waiting by the ramp, ready to greet Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan. The Chinese leader took his time to emerge into public view, and when he did, there was no stuttering or hesitation. A confident and fit-looking Xi came down the stairs and shook Trump’s hand. Among the many signals, one definitive message was the dismissal of rumours about his health.

I was up all night watching the developments because these little details matter. This breaking of normal protocol, the laying out of the red carpet and the full paraphernalia by the American side will be read in Beijing not merely as hospitality but as proof that China now commands a degree of equality with the United States.

For the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party, these minute details are a meticulously choreographed exercise in narrative control. China’s overwhelming objective for this summit is not merely to show that Beijing stands on an equal footing with Washington. It is to visually and politically validate Xi’s ideological conviction that the world is experiencing “great changes unseen in a century”, and at the heart of this shift lies the axiomatic rise of the East and the decline of the West.

Unlike Trump, who likes to play it by ear, the Chinese side would have choreographed every handshake, every pause, every scheduled photo opportunity and every concession that may be extracted during Xi’s three-day state visit. The larger objective is to prove to the world that the historical centre of global gravity has permanently shifted across the Pacific.

Therefore, Trump’s decision to meet Xi on the runway, followed by a grand military ceremony, gives Beijing exactly the affirmation it needs. For a Chinese leadership that has long insisted that the US must respect China’s “core interests”, the symbolism is itself a diplomatic achievement.

Xi will likely present China as the responsible custodian of what the two governments have called a relationship of “constructive strategic stability”, a new framework to define bilateral ties. The Chinese embassy in the US even shared a neat little graphic of it on X, timed to coincide with Xi’s arrival in Washington DC, demonstrating the importance of this framework for Beijing.

Ahead of President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States from Sept. 23 to 25, #China-#US relations enter a new moment of high-level engagement. Following the presidents’ Beijing meeting in May, the upcoming visit will spotlight dialogue, cooperation and managing… pic.twitter.com/zXJeKtfjVk
— Chinese Embassy in US (@ChineseEmbinUS) September 22, 2026
The phrase is deceptively bland, but consequential. Beijing wants a relationship with predictable limits: fewer sudden tariffs, fewer export-control escalations, fewer steps around Taiwan that China interprets as challenges to its sovereignty, and more regular leader-level diplomacy. Xi will be keen to secure Trump’s endorsement of the framework — not merely as a summit phrase, but as a shared political commitment that can guide relations beyond the visit.

Xi arrives for the talks armed with potent leverage in the form of rare earths and critical minerals. The Busan arrangement of October 2025 saw Washington pause its tariffs, while Beijing suspended a sweeping package of export controls on rare earths, magnets and critical minerals. That truce expires in early November.

Media reports indicate both sides have settled on a two-month extension. “We met today to see if we could ⁠do a bigger deal as opposed to just a series of smaller things. We ⁠have agreed today that we will extend what we call the ⁠Busan Agreement till January 10”, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was quoted as saying by Fox News on Wednesday after his meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.

China has already engineered a squeeze on exports of critical minerals to the US, with its supply of rare earth magnets falling to 512 tonnes in August, 13 per cent lower than the same month a year earlier and 20 per cent lower than in July. There is a possibility that China may use the shipments as leverage to loosen America’s ban on the export of advanced semiconductor chips. This may trigger fierce bargaining during negotiations and may ratchet up tensions if not handled well.

But no issue will carry more importance for Xi than Taiwan, the “core of the core red lines”. The proposed $14 billion US arms package for Taiwan has been delayed despite congressional pre-approval. Trump has also openly described future arms sales as a potentially useful negotiating chip and questioned why the US should risk conflict over an island “9,500 miles” away.

Xi will see an opening. He may insist on suspending the arms transfer, at the very least keeping it frozen, and getting Trump to say that he “opposes Taiwan’s independence”. If Xi can obtain even a pause, a new consultation practice, or language suggesting that Washington accepts China’s framing of Taiwan as the “source of instability”, Beijing would see it as a significant political gain.

Among the areas of convergence, AI might provide a rare opportunity. Both governments have reasons to establish narrow guardrails around increasing AI risks, and preparations for a bilateral AI safety dialogue are reportedly under way. A modest cooperative mechanism is plausible. Trump’s personal interest in the subject, however, appears limited.

Trump’s priorities lie elsewhere. Beset by negative headlines and falling popularity ratings, and facing the prospect of a Republican drubbing at the midterms, Trump needs a grand spectacle to enthral his Maga base. Trump also wants an uninterrupted Chinese supply of rare earths and critical minerals and substantial Chinese purchases of US agricultural products (very important for rural Maga voters).

A package involving mineral supplies, tariff reductions and agricultural buying would give Trump material for a victory lap. This is where Xi’s advantage becomes clearest. Trump’s objectives are proximate and tangible; Xi is playing the long game, laying out a structure that would freeze the modalities of bilateral ties in favour of Beijing.

Trump is looking for ‘deals’ and a headline. Xi wants a relationship that makes China harder to pressure. Trump wants minerals to keep flowing and soybeans to keep moving. Xi wants the US to accept, even if quietly, that Beijing holds the upper hand in this transient period of strategic stalemate.

(Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Trump’s UNGA speech sparks fresh friction with India
editorials.passage:
The United Nations General Assembly was founded in 1945 on the ashes of global conflict, designed explicitly to act as a shield against unilateral aggression and to promote international cooperation. However, when President Donald Trump stepped up to the green-marble rostrum at the UN General Assembly, the contrast between his worldview and the institution's call for global unity could not have been more pronounced. Rather than adopting the traditional, diplomatic vernacular of a world summit, Trump delivered a speech that mirrored a domestic political rally—blending boasts about American economic achievements with aggressive geopolitical ultimatums.
The Iran Conflict
The most alarming signal from the podium was Trump’s direct threat regarding the ongoing seven-month war involving the U.S., Israel, and Iran. Framing the conflict around a "big decision" to be made following the U.S. midterm elections, Trump presented a stark ultimatum: Iran must either capitulate to a new deal or face complete "annihilation".

While defenders may view such rhetoric as a classic brinkmanship tactic to force Tehran to the negotiating table, using the UN General Assembly—a body dedicated to global peace—to casually threaten the total destruction of a sovereign nation shocked many delegates. It indicated that the United States willing to bypass traditional rules of engagement, heightening the risk of catastrophic escalation in an already volatile West Asia.

‘To the victor go the spoils’
Touting a recent oil agreement following the military ousting of Venezuela's authoritarian leader earlier in the year, Trump directly cited a notorious page of American political history, stating, "To the victor go the spoils”. This statement sent a chilling message to smaller or resource-rich nations. By treating foreign national resources as literal spoils of military intervention, the speech signalled a retreat from the respect for state sovereignty that has underpinned international relations for decades. It replaced democratic idealism with a doctrine of raw resource extraction, validating fears that American intervention is fundamentally driven by commercial and territorial gain.


Why India is annoyed
Trump’s speech contained two specific, highly sensitive claims that directly challenged India’s official geopolitical stances and national sovereignty. India was reportedly annoyed by the following statements:

1) Trump again claimed during his address that his administration successfully resolved eight major international conflicts, highlighting his personal mediation in the brief 2025 India-Pakistan military confrontation. Trump referred to Pakistan as a "great country" and called PM Shehbaz Sharif a "terrific man" and an excellent person. Trump stated that Sharif called to thank him and credited his administration's intervention with helping bring an end to a military conflict between Pakistan and India in May 2025, claiming it "saved 30 million lives".

This narrative stands in stark contrast to the stance of New Delhi. The Indian government has repeatedly rejected any claims of third-party US mediation, firmly maintaining that the May 2025 ceasefire was negotiated strictly through direct, bilateral military-to-military channels between the Directors General of Military Operations of both countries. While Trump likely meant this as a boast of his prowess as a global peacemaker, New Delhi historically rejects third-party mediation regarding its bilateral relations with Pakistan.

This signals that India must continuously manage Trump’s unpredictable, personalised style of diplomacy, ensuring that its sovereign security interests are not compromised by Washington's transactional deals.


2) In his speech, Trump directly singled out China and India as the primary funders of the Russia-Ukraine war. He targeted India for its continued purchase of discounted Russian crude oil, reiterating a long-standing grievance that New Delhi's energy trade fills Moscow's war chests.

Trump's remarks rubbed salt into an existing wound; the Trump administration had previously waged a tariff war against India—imposing severe 50 per cent duties on certain Indian exports as a penalty for buying Russian oil—before partially dialling them back under an ongoing trade negotiation. India has consistently defended its oil imports from Russia as a pragmatic necessity to protect its own energy security and shield its large population from global inflation spikes. Trump's aggravated friction points in the Washington–New Delhi relationship by publicly questioning India's strategic autonomy.
Rejection of Globalist Frameworks
In his address, President Donald Trump delivered a blunt reassertion of American sovereignty that explicitly rejected several key global frameworks and international bodies. Centring his message on an "America First" doctrine, Trump forcefully pushed back against multilateral oversight, declaring that the United States “totally rejects” any international attempt to construct a globalist scheme to regulate artificial intelligence. His remarks directly countered a call by UN Secretary-General António Guterres for a global AI management framework.

Beyond technology, Trump renewed sharp criticisms of long-standing global institutions, labelling the International Criminal Court (ICC) an institution "full of evil people" with no authority over the US, while urging other nations to withdraw from it. He further targeted the UN Human Rights Council, UNESCO, and the International Maritime Organisation, arguing that these bodies should not advance global governance or override sovereign independent actions. Asserting that "there is no global government" and promising to block any form of global taxation, Trump framed unilateral military and economic resolve as the only credible path to security, effectively signalling a profound disregard for traditional multilateral cooperation.

Conclusion
Donald Trump's address to the 81st UN General Assembly went beyond standard political rhetoric. It signalled a fundamental erosion of international norms. By threatening total annihilation, bragging about the "spoils" of war, and rejecting collective oversight on critical future technologies like AI, the speech presented a bleak outlook on global stability. For a global audience watching from the UN floor, the message was unmistakable: the world's most powerful nation is increasingly pivoting away from diplomacy, favouring a philosophy of raw power and unilateral action.

(The writer is a retired Indian diplomat and had previously served as ambassador in Kuwait and Morocco and as consul general in New York. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Prime Minister Modi Owes India's Daughters an Apology
editorials.passage: Prime Minister Narendra Modi owes Indian women a video apology. I don’t care which angle he shoots it from, where and at what time he releases it, what slang he uses in an attempt to connect with us, whether or not he’s aided by a teleprompter, or what he chooses to wear when he finally tells us he’s sorry.Of course, it won’t have quite the same ring as “I am just 15. Forgive me.” Yes, that’s what a teenager was compelled to say with folded hands after she expressed what she thinks about him, using expletives at the recent NEET-linked student protests at Jantar Mantar. “I apologise to the entire country. I am so ashamed. I can’t even look at myself. Please forgive me,” she said in a video.It’s time PM Modi returned the favour to the young women of this country who have faced so much unchecked violence since he came to power—some of it in the days after the PM and his coterie were busy getting the country to light diyas to celebrate his birthday.Please don’t make me devote a paragraph to the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) data again.The assault by a group of men in Bihar’s Jamui on a 15-year-old student returning from a coaching class occurred just two days after the PM’s birthday. As is always the case in New India, the crime was recorded and distributed for enjoyment. Two days after this, a 17-year-old was gang raped in a Delhi park by a group posing as policemen—just 2 km from her elite college. It was her birthday too, sir. But we know PM Modi will not engage with the student protestors of Lady Shri Ram College who are correctly pointing out that women’s safety isn’t just our responsibility. Modi's Remarks on Abuse Overlook a Decade of His Supporters' ConductWho remembers the PM's feminist posturing from the ramparts of the Red Fort on his first Independence Day speech in 2014, grandly tossing the sweeping tail of his saffron turban that overshadowed its green border? He framed rape as an issue of national shame, and even urged Indians to adopt new parenting standards. “If every parent decides to impose as many restrictions on the sons as have been imposed on our daughters, try to do this with your sons, try to ask such questions of them,” he said. Cue clapping.But nobody reined in their raja betas or even hinted to their sons that they should stop raping and attacking other people’s daughters who they may encounter in public spaces. Money was collected in a scheme named after us, most of it was spent on advertising directed at ‘saving’ Indian betis—and nothing changed.Surely our widely travelled PM knows that the issue of violence against women cannot be solved by commissioning some generic advertising with alliterative slogans?PM Modi remembered us again in his annual address in 2022, after COVID-19—a time when crimes against women and girls skyrocketed as we were locked down with our abusers. This time he asked people to take a “pledge” to stop “insulting” women, his language intentionally understating the every day violence we face. “The more opportunities we give to our daughters, the more they will take India forward,” he said. Forget thriving or succeeding, we fight to survive in this country. PM Modi should explain why he doesn’t think safeguarding half this country’s population is an issue worthy of his time and effort.BJP's Winning Formula: Women Voters & Welfare SchemesSomeone remind him he’s a PM, not a priest. It’s okay to preach about pledges and parenting styles and repackage words like ‘sindoor’ in pithy quotes and as titles of military operations, but the real work begins after a politician steps down from the pulpit. Yet, PM Modi follows the worst misogynists on X. You won’t find him standing up for women in the case of Brij Bhushan vs Indian women or in the case of Himanshi Narwal, whose naval officer husband was killed in the Pahalgam attack. He doesn’t react to the misogynistic language used by elected office-bearers in his party, maybe because his own anti-woman language is well-documented. Muslims should bring their sisters and daughters to garba, Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) MLA Rameshwar Sharma said earlier this week. “Our boys are also ready.” We know PM Modi won’t say anything about this rape threat. And yes, let’s not forget he endorsed The Kerala Story, a wild conspiracy movie that portrays women as the property of men and having no agency or intelligence of their own. Two of his Hindi belt chief ministers even made the movie tax-free in their states.Meanwhile, the country ruled by this strongman has become even more violent and patriarchal as Hindutva foot soldiers online (and offline) stalk, disrespect, and abuse women, especially from marginalised and minority communities. They coordinate online attacks against women in public office and those who criticise the government.Assaulted, Not Silenced: Muslim Women Journalists Who Refused to Be IntimidatedVocal Muslim women were ‘sold’ in faux online auctions on apps with names like Bulli Bai and Sulli Deals. “This type of continuous digital violence numbs public conscience,” writes Saadia Azim in Forwarded As Received: How Misinformation Turns Viral, Violent and True. “It normalises trauma and repackages systematic harassment as harmless humour.” Well, we’ve had enough of ‘harmless’ humour.The PM will have to tell us how he plans to tackle VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN and RAPE CULTURE. I know you’re NOT comfortable with apologies, sir, but it’s never too late to learn a new skill.So, switch on that video. Show us some genuine remorse. Own up to your missteps. Don’t be reluctant or grudging. Avoid the passive voice. Don’t say “I’m sorry if…” And tell us what you are going to do to fix the problem.Or else we will have to fix it ourself. As you famously tweeted in 2013 after the gang rape of Jyoti Singh: “When you go to vote—think—they made my Delhi a rape capital.”Keep fighting girls. One day he will have to hear us.Predictably, the Delhi government has restricted access to public parks after sunset. Somebody remind the PM to tell his team that parks don’t rape women. Neither do buses. Or coaching centres.(The author is the founder of India Love Project and on the editorial board of Article 14. This is an opinion piece. All views expressed are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for them.)  Parliament Has Learned Gen Z Slang. But Has it Learned to Listen to Them?
